- SE is true exactly if people find cool, glacial **H2O** more refreshing than warm, swamp H2O, and if there were no clean H2O people could not survive.
- TS is true exactly if people find cool, glacial **XYZ** more refreshing than warm, swamp XYZ, and if there were no clean XYZ people could not survive.

So SE and TS express different propositions. Their truth-conditions differ. And yet Smith and Twin-Smith are, by hypothesis, psychologically identical.

That yields Putnam’s thesis:

> **PTM**: the meanings borne by our utterances are not determined solely by the thoughts we have; there is a strictly non-psychological, strictly environmental dimension to linguistic meaning.

## Competence without chemistry

A predictable objection now arises. If “water” refers to H2O as a matter of semantics, must not mastery of English require knowledge of the chemical composition of water? And similarly for gold, lead, aluminum, and so on? That would be absurd.

The reply depends on distinguishing a semantic rule from the information by means of which one grasps that rule.

Take the name “Barack Obama.” There is some individual x such that the semantic rule is:

- “Barack Obama” refers to x.

If one does not know which individual that is, one does not know the semantic rule. But there are indefinitely many ways of singling out that same x. The example given is “Jack Jones.” Let P1, P2, P3, and so on be predicates each uniquely satisfied by Jack Jones. If Smith knows:

- there is some x such that x uniquely satisfies P75 and “Jack Jones” refers to x,

while Jones knows:

- there is some x such that x uniquely satisfies P143 and “Jack Jones” refers to x,

then Smith and Jones are nevertheless in complete semantic accord. They attach the name to the same person. When either says “Jack Jones has psi,” what each intends is simply to attribute psi to x. Neither wishes to say anything about his own way of thinking about x.

Exactly parallel points hold for “water.” One may know what “water” refers to by knowing any truth of the form:

- there is some substance x such that x uniquely has property phi, and “water” refers to x.

The italicized part alone describes the semantic rule. The rest gives the route by which one grasps that rule. Thus one does not need chemistry to know English. Smith may know that water is what is in bathtubs and drinking glasses; Jones may know that water is H2O and the medium in which creatures with gills can breathe. If both know that “water” refers to the same substance x, then when each says “water covers most of the Earth’s surface,” each means that x covers most of the Earth’s surface. Differences in mode of presentation do not jeopardize communication.

This distinction between **literal meaning** and the information through which a speaker grasps a referent is crucial for everything that follows.

## From semantic externalism to Burge’s blunder

Putnam’s conclusion is correct. Smith’s words and Twin-Smith’s words differ in literal meaning though Smith and Twin-Smith have the same thoughts. Under pressure from Burge, Putnam later abandoned this correct insight. Burge’s move is from **semantic externalism** to **content-externalism**: not only do Smith’s and Twin-Smith’s words differ in meaning, Burge says, their thoughts differ in content.

The chapter’s central claim is that this move is a blunder.

Burge’s example is “arthritis.” On Earth, “arthritis” refers to a disease exclusively of the joints. On Twin-Earth, “arthritis” refers to a similar but distinct ailment afflicting not only joints but also certain bones. Let that ailment be “twin-arthritis.”

Smith on Earth sincerely accepts:

- “arthritis is unpleasant.”

Twin-Smith on Twin-Earth sincerely accepts the same sentence. Burge concludes that Smith is thinking about arthritis, while Twin-Smith is thinking about twin-arthritis, so their thought-contents differ despite psychological identity.

The reply mirrors the reply in the water case. How does Smith learn “arthritis”? Someone says:

> “the unpleasant inflammation in your knees is due to arthritis; arthritis can do terrible damage to one’s joints.”

This communicates something like:

- there is some x such that the swelling in your knees is due to x and x can do terrible damage to one’s joints; moreover, “arthritis” refers to x.

When Smith hears “arthritis has psi,” the message communicated, though not literally meant, is tied to that way of picking out the referent. Since Twin-Smith’s life parallels Smith’s exactly, the same message is communicated to Twin-Smith. Therefore, contrary to Burge, Smith’s thought-content and Twin-Smith’s thought-content coincide.

What differs is the **literal meaning** of the sentence-token “arthritis is painful” on Earth and Twin-Earth. On Earth it is true iff arthritis is painful; on Twin-Earth it is true iff twin-arthritis is painful. But it does not follow that the thoughts behind the utterances differ. Burge’s mistake is to assume too tight a connection between literal meaning and **cognitive content**.

## Literal meaning versus cognitive content

This distinction becomes even clearer in the Max-Gary case. Let W1 be a world where, at time t, I am ten feet from Max and say while pointing:

- “That entity is wearing a plaid shirt.”

Call this utterance **U1**. Let W2 be exactly like W1 except that I am looking not at Max but at Gary, Max’s identical twin, and produce **U2**:

- “That entity is wearing a plaid shirt.”

The truth-conditions of the utterances differ:

- U1 is true iff Max is wearing a plaid shirt.
- U2 is true iff Gary is wearing a plaid shirt.

These are different propositions. So the literal meanings differ.

Burge-style reasoning says: therefore the thoughts differ. In W1 I think of Max; in W2 I think of Gary. The chapter rejects this. To expose the mistake, add W3. In W3 the thing before me is neither Max nor Gary but a robot that looks exactly like both. I do not know robots like this exist. I see the robot and say:

- “That entity is wearing a plaid shirt.”

Call this **U3**. My visual perception here is **VR**.

VR is high-resolution and veridical. It tells me accurately how the thing before me looks. But it does not, by itself, tell me whether I am seeing Max, Gary, or some third thing. The content delivered by perception is therefore **existential** and general:

> **CVR**: There is some entity x such that x has such and such characteristics, such that x is standing in a certain place and such that x is wearing a plaid shirt.

That is the relevant belief embodied in U3. It is correct whether the thing is Max, Gary, or a robot. Hence:

1. There is no particular x such that VR tells me it is x specifically that I am seeing.
2. There is no particular x such that the belief embodied in U3 is correct only if x is wearing a plaid shirt.

And because the experiential situations in W1, W2, and W3 are indistinguishable, the same existential content, CVR, is the content of the perceptions and beliefs underlying U1 and U2 as well. Russell’s remark makes the point: experience itself does not guarantee identity across occasions; a similar table may be substituted without altering experience.

So U1, U2, and U3 have different literal meanings, but the thought embodied in them—the belief based strictly on perception—is the same. Burge’s error is his failure to distinguish what we know directly from perception from what we infer from perception using background knowledge.

If, while looking at Gary, I also know independently that nothing other than Gary looks quite like Gary, then I may know that I am seeing Gary. But that knowledge is not delivered by perception alone; it is perception plus background knowledge. The content of the perception itself remains existential and identity-neutral.

## Hallucination and the gappiness of Burge thoughts

The deepest problem for Burge emerges with hallucination. Let W4 be like W1–W3 except that there is no person before me at all: Sally and I are hallucinating. My hallucination, **VH**, is phenomenologically just like the perception in the other worlds, and prompted by it I utter:

- “That entity is wearing a plaid shirt.”

Call this **U4**.

U4 is not true or false. It is **abortive**. The model is Strawson’s point about:

- “that gnome weighs 8 lbs”

uttered while pointing to a non-existent gnome. The utterance presupposes there is such a gnome; since there is not, it is neither true nor false. By contrast,

- “there is a gnome on my bed, and that gnome weighs 8 lbs”

is false.

Burge rightly agrees that U4 fails to encode a proposition. But he infers that VH itself has no content; it gives only a fragment:

> **BLNK**: ___ is wearing a plaid shirt.

Likewise, the thought based on VH supposedly contains a blank. This is the doctrine of the **gappiness** of Burge thoughts.

The chapter’s objection is direct: this is preposterous. VH obviously gives a complete message. It tells me, falsely, that there is some entity in a certain place wearing a plaid shirt. That is precisely CVR. False messages are still complete messages. Since BLNK is neither true nor false whereas the message actually delivered by hallucination is false, Burge’s account fails.

The result is intolerable. If Burge were right, then in W4, when asked what I am thinking, I would be wrong to answer: “I’m thinking that the fellow standing over there is wearing a plaid shirt.” But plainly I do know what I am consciously thinking, even though what I think is false.

## Descartes and privileged knowledge of thought

The same problem generalizes to thoughts about Descartes. Suppose that right now, at time t, I am thinking:

- **D\***: Descartes was a fine philosopher.

Suppose later it is discovered that Descartes never existed, that the records were all forged. On Burge’s causal conception of conception, I think about Descartes only if my thought causally tracks back to Descartes. If Descartes never existed, no such tracking relation exists. Then D\* does not merely become false; it does not exist to be thought. The mental events that seemed to constitute my thinking D\* would, in that case, constitute no thought at all.

This yields the absurd consequence that two psychologically identical individuals could differ in that one is thinking D\* while the other is thinking nothing at all—a zombie or blank where a thought should be. But thought is psychological activity. So Burge’s view implies that thought is not a psychological process. The chapter deems this not only false but incoherent.

Burge admits three points:

1. It is possible, given only my mental states, that Descartes never existed.
2. If Descartes existed and I am thinking D\*, then there is some individual x = Descartes such that D\* is correct iff x was a fine philosopher.
3. If I were in the very same mental state but Descartes had never existed, then I would not be thinking D\* at all.

From these Burge is committed to:

4. If I am now thinking D\*, I cannot be more certain that I am thinking D\* than I am that Descartes existed.

But that is obviously wrong. I know my current conscious thought more certainly than I know facts about seventeenth-century France. Burge’s theory therefore undermines the evident asymmetry between knowledge of one’s own present thought and knowledge of remote facts about the external world.

## Fodor’s insight and causal impotence

A further objection concerns causation. If Smith and Twin-Smith are psychologically and physiologically identical, then their thoughts have the same causal properties. The supposed difference in externally individuated content makes no difference to behavior or internal psychological process. It is causally inert.

Fodor’s insight is to state a criterion for sameness of causal properties: two things x and y are causally identical if, were they switched while all else remained unchanged, each would behave as the other does. Atom-for-atom duplicate billiard balls illustrate the point. Different effects in different contexts do not show different causal powers; they show one set of causal powers operating under different surrounding conditions.

The chapter adds a stronger claim: **causality is indistinguishable from spatiotemporal existence**. To occupy space-time is already to have causal properties. So if the alleged difference between Smith’s thought-content and Twin-Smith’s is wholly without causal consequence, it makes no sense to posit it as something real.

Burge replies by denying Fodor’s criterion. He says causal properties should be understood by what objects actually do in their environments, not by what they would do in counterfactual circumstances. His example is that two atom-for-atom duplicate celestial bodies can differ because one is a planet and one is not.

But the reply in the chapter is that this conflates an object with the fact of its being embedded in a certain environment. A’s being a planet is not identical with A; it is a state of affairs involving A. So differences in what A and B do, due to different environmental embedding, do not establish differences in the intrinsic causal properties of A and B themselves. Likewise, differences in behavior explained by Smith’s being an uncle and Jones’s not being one do not show that Smith and Jones differ intrinsically as persons.

Hence Burge’s strategy fails. The content-differences he posits are explanatorily idle and causally impotent.

## The final lesson

Putnam’s insight should therefore be preserved in its original form. The Twin-Earth cases show that **literal meaning** is partly environmentally determined. They do not show that psychologically identical individuals differ in **cognitive content**. Burge’s mistake is to collapse the distinction between what utterances literally mean and what speakers think or communicate through them. Once that distinction is restored, Putnam’s semantic externalism remains a profound truth, while Burge’s content-externalism collapses under its own consequences: blanks in thought, the denial of our obvious knowledge of our present conscious thinking, and causally inert pseudo-differences that make no sense as constituents of psychological reality.

title: Hyper-Justified True Belief
blurb: Knowledge is not mere justified true belief, but true belief whose justification correctly explains the data.
body:
# Hyper-Justified True Belief

## The ambiguity of “know”

The word **know** is ambiguous. Sometimes it refers to awareness of objects, as in “I know Smith.” Sometimes it refers to awareness of truths, as in “I know that snow is white.” This is not a trivial linguistic quirk. Some languages distinguish these by different verbs: Spanish uses *conocer* for knowing people and *saber* for knowing truths; German uses *kennen* and *wissen*. English and Russian do not mark the distinction in this way. That convergence suggests that the failure sharply to distinguish knowledge of people from knowledge of truths reflects something epistemologically real rather than a mere accident of grammar.

The chapter’s governing suggestion is therefore striking: knowledge of people is, at least often, knowledge of truths. We will eventually see why. For now, the focal sense of knowledge is knowledge of truths.

There is another ambiguity worth marking immediately. Philosophers and psychologists often speak of **procedural knowledge**: knowing how to do something. The ability to play the piano, to speak English, or to tie one’s shoes are cases of this. Many deny that such knowledge is bona fide knowledge. The chapter insists on the contrary. What the virtuoso knows procedurally, the incompetent neophyte knows only discursively. As knowledge deepens, it becomes proceduralized. **Non-procedural knowledge** is poorly integrated knowledge; procedural knowledge is sufficiently integrated to be mobilized. So it is indefensible to deny that procedural knowledge is knowledge.

Still, unless explicitly stated otherwise, “knowledge” here means knowledge of truths.

## Knowledge as justified true belief

Three claims are immediately unavoidable.

1. One cannot know what is false.
2. If one knows something, one believes it.
3. Not all beliefs are knowledge.

The first point is elementary but important. People may feel equally certain of a falsehood and a truth. The intensity of belief does not distinguish truth from falsity. But only truths can be known.

The second point is equally straightforward. If someone said, non-ironically, “I know that Paris is the capital of France, but I don’t believe it,” the utterance would be nonsense. Knowledge entails belief.

The third point introduces the traditional analysis. Not every belief, even every true belief, is knowledge. A belief must also be **justified**.

The multiple-choice example makes this plain:

> With what digit does Professor Kuczynski’s phone number end?  
> (a) 9  
> (b) 3  
> (c) 2  
> (d) 0  
> (e) none of the above

A lucky guess may earn credit on the test, but it does not amount to knowledge. If the chosen answer is right only by accident, then one has no knowledge. One must have good reason for one’s answer: perhaps the number was told to one, appeared on a handout, or was discovered by a private detective. These are sources of justification.

Moreover, not every route to a true belief counts. If one falsely believes that all people with red hair have cancer, and on that basis concludes that one’s red-haired friend Bob has cancer, then even if Bob really does have cancer, one does not know this. Why not? Because the reason is **spurious**. False premises can lead to true conclusions; misinformation can produce a correct belief. But when that happens, the truth is reached accidentally.

So knowledge initially appears to require three conditions:

1. the belief must be true;
2. it must be believed;
3. it must be justified.

Thus all cases of knowledge are cases of **justified true belief**.

## Sources of justification

What constitutes justification? The chapter identifies three ultimate sources.

First, **perceptual evidence**: evidence deriving from sense-perception—sight, hearing, taste, smell, bodily sensation, and also sensations of motion and resistance. One knows there is a computer in front of one because one sees it; knows the stove is hot because one touched it; knows one cup is heavier than another because one feels greater resistance in moving it.

Second, **introspective evidence**: one’s direct awareness of one’s own mental contents. One may know one is thinking about the theory of knowledge, this chapter, and tonight’s dinner. This is not sensory knowledge, nor does it seem inferential. It seems to be direct, non-inferential awareness of one’s own thoughts.

Third, **rational inference**: knowledge derived from other things one is justified in believing.

These three—perceptual evidence, introspective evidence, and rational inference—are the basic sources of justification. Different categories of fact draw on them differently. Some knowledge involves only inference; some combines perception and introspection; much combines perception and inference.

## Testimony as justified belief

A large amount of what one knows is not personally verified. One knows it because one is told. Testimony may take the form of speech, writing, photographs, drawings, and so on. I have not seen the Earth from outer space, yet I know that it is approximately spherical because I have been told it.

But testimony is not automatically justificatory. For testimony-based belief to qualify as knowledge, two conditions are necessary:

1. the testimony must come from a **reliable source**;
2. the recipient must have **independent evidence** of that source’s reliability.

The cult example displays the failure of these conditions. Suppose one’s cult leader says that a beverage is extremely nutritious. The beverage really is nutritious, and one believes this. Yet one has no evidence that the cult leader is informed or truthful; one believes him for purely emotional reasons. Then one has a true belief, but not knowledge.

By contrast, if a world-renowned physician says one has arthritis, his opinion rests on expertise and tests, and one knows both that he is an expert and that he conducted the tests, then one’s testimony-based belief can be knowledge.

So testimony-based knowledge is possible, but only where the source’s reliability is itself supported. Such knowledge combines perception and inference: one perceives the words, perceives evidence of the source’s truthfulness, and infers reliability.

A subtle point then arises about childhood learning. As children, we accept much from parents and teachers before we have independent corroboration. We are inclined to say that we knew these things. The chapter’s suggestion is harsher: at first, we did not know them; we merely believed them. Later we either acquired evidence of the speaker’s reliability or discovered the facts ourselves.

## Gettier and the failure of justified true belief

The traditional three-part analysis is necessary but not sufficient. This is the central turning point.

One can have a justified true belief that is not knowledge. Gettier’s example shows this. You know Smith is an excellent worker, liked by the boss, due for promotion; you know the boss has announced a promotion; you also know Smith drives a Ford. On this basis you form the belief:

> somebody who drives a Ford is about to be given a promotion.

This belief is justified. It also turns out true. But Smith does not get the promotion; Jones gets it, because the boss owes a huge favor to Jones’s exceptionally vindictive Mafia-boss father. By coincidence, Jones also drives a Ford.

So the belief is:

1. true;
2. believed;
3. justified.

Yet it is not knowledge, because it is true for the wrong reason. The truth of the belief is only accidentally connected to its justification.

Russell’s broken clock case makes the same point. One looks at a clock that is in fact broken, though one has every reason to think it works. It reads 4:00 P.M., and by fluke that is the actual time. The belief is true and justified, but not knowledge.

The lesson is that a fourth condition is required.

## Knowledge as non-accidentally justified true belief

The needed condition is initially expressed approximately:

4. there must be a **non-accidental connection** between one’s justification for the belief and the fact that makes the belief true.

So knowledge is not merely justified true belief but **non-accidentally justified true belief**. Yet this is still too vague. What does “non-accidentally” mean here?

The clock case allows refinement. In the broken-clock example, one’s immediate justification is:

- the clock is now telling me that it’s 4:00 P.M.

But that by itself does not justify the belief. The deeper justification is one’s background belief:

- in my extensive past experience, the clock has always been right, and the building superintendent is capable and diligent; these facts ensured that if the clock says a certain time, that is because it really is that time.

This is an **explanation** of why the clock is now reading 4:00. But it is the wrong explanation. The right explanation is that the clock is broken and always reads 4:00.

This sets up the decisive notion.

## Hyper-justification

Consider now the Larry-in-Texas case. You see Larry get on a plane apparently bound for Texas. Later he calls from next to a well-known Texas landmark, or a perfect duplicate of one. On this basis you believe Larry is in Texas, and he is.

Now compare two worlds.

In the “real world,” what happened is exactly what you think happened. Larry flew to Texas and called you from there. Your belief is justified, and your belief also gives the correct explanation of the data—the images and noises from the call.

In the **Alternative Scenario**, Martians reroute the plane to Barbados, transport Larry to Texas, and then someone other than Larry who looks and sounds exactly like him calls you from Texas. Your belief that Larry is in Texas is still true and justified, but it is not knowledge. Why? Because your belief does not correctly explain the data. Your account of why the images and noises are occurring is false.

This leads to the chapter’s proposed refinement: a belief is **hyper-justified** if it is justified and also **embodies a correct explanation of the data that is doing the justifying**.

Hence the proposed analysis:

- **Knowledge is hyper-justified true belief.**

That is the chapter’s preferred formulation of the fourth condition. The connection between truth and justification must not merely be non-accidental in some unspecified sense; the belief must correctly explain the very data that justifies it.

## Analytic and synthetic knowledge

Knowledge divides into **analytic** and **synthetic**.

**Analytic knowledge** is purely conceptual. One knows it by analyzing the statement or its constituent concepts. The example is:

> Circles are figures of uniform curvature.

One becomes justified in believing this by examining the concepts *circle*, *curvature*, *uniform*, and so on. Statement-analysis suffices.

**Synthetic knowledge** has a non-conceptual component. Consider:

> Donald Rumsfeld was born in the United States.

No amount of conceptual analysis will determine whether this is true. One must consult facts: birth records, informed testimony, and so forth.

The chapter further proposes, controversially but explicitly, that synthetic knowledge is identical with **knowledge of spatiotemporal facts**, while analytic knowledge is knowledge of **properties**. Thus knowing that Rumsfeld was born in the United States is knowing something about the spatiotemporal world; knowing that circles are figures of uniform curvature is knowing an unchanging relation among properties.

## Knowledge of facts and of laws

Within synthetic knowledge there is an important division between:

1. knowledge of **specific facts**;
2. knowledge of **causal or nomic relations** among facts.

A **nomic** relation is one having to do with natural law. Combustion when a lit match contacts gasoline is not coincidence; it reflects a principled dependence. The **covering law** for a causal sequence is the natural law of which that sequence is an instance.

Knowledge of natural law is still synthetic. It is not reached by conceptual analysis. Even obvious-seeming laws, such as unsupported objects falling, are synthetic; they merely feel obvious because the relevant spatiotemporal knowledge constantly forces itself upon us.

## Knowledge of future, past, and counterfactuals

Knowledge of the future requires two ingredients:

1. knowledge of present conditions;
2. knowledge of causal laws linking those conditions to future outcomes.

If I know there is water in the pitcher, know that an open overturned pitcher containing non-viscous liquid will release it under relevant conditions, and know that I intend to tip the pitcher, then I can know that water will soon flow into the glass.

Indirect knowledge of the past has the same structure, but reversed. We project backward from present traces using causal laws. Inky lines on paper, together with the knowledge that pressing an ink-filled pen against paper leaves such lines and that they are unlikely to arise otherwise, justify the belief that someone dragged a pen across the paper.

Knowledge of **counterfactuals**—what would have been—is likewise knowledge of relations of dependence. To know

> if Smith had fallen off the ledge, he would now be dead or severely injured

is to know a causal law linking falls from great heights to injury or death. To know

> if x were a square, x would have four sides

is to know a logical dependence.

The chapter forcefully rejects the view that counterfactuals are made true by events in other universes. That is described as preposterous. Knowledge of what would happen in other worlds is parasitic on prior modal knowledge in this world. What makes a true counterfactual true is entirely located in this world.

## Theoretical, inferential, and perceptual knowledge

A **theory** is an explanation of what is directly experienced in terms of what is not directly experienced. Thus knowledge of electrons or the unconscious is theoretical. We know effects relatively directly; we posit unobservables to explain them.

All theoretical knowledge is inferential, but not all inferential knowledge is theoretical. If I infer fire from smoke, the inference is not theoretical. It rests on an observable concomitance, not an integrated explanatory theory of unobservables. But inferring unconscious hostility from accident-proneness presupposes a theory of the psyche and is therefore theoretical.

The chapter also entertains the strong possibility that even perceptual knowledge is theoretical. The mind receives mere disturbances of sensory surfaces and somehow transforms them into accurate perceptual representations. The gulf between input and perceptual output resembles the gulf bridged by scientific theory. A second reason comes from size perception: from a hundred feet away, a stop sign’s appearance underdetermines whether it is near and small, far and enormous, or ordinary-sized at ordinary distance. Background knowledge helps constitute one’s seeing it as the size and distance it is. So perception appears saturated with prior knowledge.

This supports the thesis of **a priori knowledge**: knowledge coded into the structure of the mind and therefore pre-existing perception. If perceptual knowledge itself presupposes such structures, then some knowledge must be innate. Plato, Leibniz, Kant, and Chomsky affirm this; Aristotle, Locke, and Quine deny it.

## Knowledge by acquaintance and description

The chapter returns at the end to the initial ambiguity of “know.” **Knowledge by acquaintance** is awareness of objects; **knowledge by description** is awareness of truths describing them. The crucial claim is that most acquaintance collapses into description.

An **existence-claim** is a statement that some description is satisfied. The store owner’s false robbery report is an existence-claim: there exists a tall male robber with pointy gold teeth and a forehead tattoo saying “I love mom.” It is false because the description is unsatisfied. By contrast:

> There exists a person who is currently (in Feb. 2008) the U.S. president

is true because the description is satisfied by George W. Bush.

Now theoretical knowledge is plainly descriptive. We are aware of electrons only in the sense that we know the truth of existence-claims they satisfy. But the stronger thesis is that **perceptual knowledge is also descriptive**. A visual perception tells one that an existence-claim is true:

> there exists a piece of paper in such and such a location, with such and such shape and color, and such and such discolorations.

Perception is description. Therefore perceptual awareness of objects, including other people, is itself awareness of truths of a certain kind. That vindicates the opening suggestion that knowledge of objects often collapses into knowledge of truths.

The likely exception is awareness of some of one’s own psychological states. An intense pain seems not to be known via an existence-claim. It is simply there, in the theater of consciousness. So at least some self-awareness may be genuinely non-descriptive.

## Procedural, intuitive, and discursive knowledge

The same assimilative strategy is applied to **knowledge-how**. The popular argument says: knowing how to ride a bike differs fundamentally from knowing truths, since one may have the one without the other. The chapter rejects this. Knowledge of a language is a skill, but it requires semantic and syntactic knowledge-that. Thus **procedural knowledge is operationalized declarative knowledge**. It may not begin discursively, and one may lack conscious access to the declarative knowledge embedded in it, but that shows only that the mind is compartmentalized.

Finally, the chapter distinguishes **intuitive** from **discursive** knowledge. One knows intuitively when one knows without knowing how one knows. One knows discursively when one also knows one’s grounds.

Timmy sees a figure and says it is a circle but can only say, “I just know.” Jones says it is a circle because any two arbitrarily short segments of its periphery have equal curvature. Both know it is a circle. The difference is not that Timmy lacks the relevant basis altogether. Rather:

1. Jones knows, while Timmy does not, what grounds are moving him to judge as he does.
2. Jones knows the same fact under two descriptions—a sensory one and a propositional one—whereas Timmy knows it under only one.

Thus intuitive knowledge is not non-knowledge. It is often better integrated knowledge, knowledge whose justificatory basis has been internalized so thoroughly that conscious rehearsal is no longer needed.

That same point ultimately bears on discovery. The slogan that **justification isn’t discovery** is misleading. Discovery is coming to know, and knowledge requires justification. Therefore justification is internal to genuine discovery, even if the discoverer cannot fully state it, and even if others are not yet justified in accepting the result. There is often a delay between possessing a justification, knowing what it is, articulating it, and transmitting it. Confusing these is what obscures the unity of justification and discovery.

The chapter’s conception of knowledge is therefore demanding but unified. Knowledge requires truth, belief, justification, and a principled connection between justification and truth. That principled connection is captured by **hyper-justification**: the belief must correctly explain the very data that justifies it. Most awareness of objects is descriptive awareness of truths; much mature knowledge is proceduralized; intuition is often the mark not of epistemic weakness but of epistemic depth.

title: Descartes, Skepticism, and Mind
blurb: Descartes recasts philosophy around rigorous justification, skepticism, and the problem of mind and body.
body:
# Descartes, Skepticism, and Mind

## Descartes’ revolutionary standard

Pre-modern philosophy, we are told, tended to revolve around two questions: whether God exists, and whether universals exist independently of thought. A **universal** is a property or characteristic. Descartes changes the center of gravity. He does believe in God’s existence, and he thinks he knows how God’s existence is to be proved. He is not much interested in universals. What matters is that he insists that nothing should be believed unless it can be rigorously established.

That insistence is the central tenet of his work. Nothing is to be accepted on faith. Everything, including God’s existence and the legitimacy of scripture, must be justified by logical reason. This demand for rigorous establishment is what makes Descartes the founder of modern philosophy, and more specifically the inventor of analytic epistemology.

This rigor is inseparable from his mathematical ideal. Descartes, as a great mathematician and the inventor of analytic geometry, takes Euclid as his model. Euclid attempted to derive geometry from a small number of **axioms** or postulates. In Euclid’s sense, an axiom is not merely any assumption adopted for convenience, but a **self-evident truth**: something that cannot be grasped without being seen to be true, and that neither requires nor admits of justification. Descartes’ ambition is to do for all knowledge what Euclid tried to do for geometry: derive it from a few self-evident truths.

The *Meditations on First Philosophy* has two interconnected aims:

1. to axiomatize human knowledge;
2. to refute **skepticism**.

Here **skepticism** is the doctrine that we cannot establish that our sense-perceptions represent the world as it really is. Perhaps our experiences are one vast hallucination or dream. I believe I am typing on a keyboard. But how do I know this? How do I know I am not hallucinating or dreaming? Descartes’ attempt to answer this fails. Still, the structure of his attempt sets the agenda.

## Foundationalism and coherentism

In approaching the problem of hallucination and dream, the text distinguishes two broad epistemological strategies: **foundationalism** and **coherentism**.

**Foundationalism** holds that all knowledge coincides with, or rests on top of, knowledge of certain self-evident principles. Knowledge is like a building: it has a ground floor, a foundation, on which everything else rests. Aristotle is said to be a foundationalist, and so is Descartes.

**Coherentism** denies that there are foundational pieces of knowledge. There is no ground floor. Rather, given various data that are not themselves knowledge—sensations or perceptions, for example—if those data support one another in certain ways, then reasonable inferences may be made, and in favorable cases the result is knowledge.

The coherentist illustration is important. I have various experiences: I see, or think I see, a table and computer; I feel resistance when pushing the buttons on the keyboard. Similar visual experiences have in the past been accompanied by corresponding tactile experiences. These patterns are regular and predictable. My experiences, taken jointly, form a coherent and consistent picture of the world, and from that coherence I reasonably infer an external world of which they are a more or less faithful, though incomplete, picture.

So the contrast is sharp:

- For the coherentist, no single perception by itself constitutes knowledge.
- For the foundationalist, some beliefs are self-evidently correct; to have them is ipso facto to have knowledge.

Descartes is ultimately a foundationalist, though later he makes some coherentist points. In Meditation 1, however, he does not seriously entertain a coherentist answer to skepticism. Instead, he looks for **indubitable** principles.

## The cogito and privileged self-knowledge

Descartes’ first major claim is that certain beliefs about one’s own mind are self-evidently correct, whereas beliefs about external objects never have that status.

The key contrast is this:

1. I can doubt that there is an external world, because I might be perpetually hallucinating or dreaming.
2. I cannot doubt that my mind exists.

Why not? Because doubting is itself a form of mental activity. To doubt the existence of my own mind, I must have a mind. Doubt concerning the existence of mind is therefore self-undermining. Doubt concerning the existence of the external world is not: from the mere fact that I seem to see a stick, it does not follow that there is a stick there.

This is the force of “I think; therefore I am.” One cannot think without existing. Since doubting is a kind of thinking, doubting one’s own existence presupposes that one exists. This gives Descartes an **Archimedean point** from which he hopes to reconstruct all the beliefs we pretheoretically regard as true.

A second point deepens the asymmetry between self and world. If I have an experience like that of seeing a stick, it does not follow that there is a stick there. But if I have an experience like that of being in pain, then it does follow that I am in pain. An experience like pain is pain. By contrast, an experience like that of seeing a stick need not be an experience *of* a stick. The text judges Descartes to overgeneralize this point if he extends it to all self-knowledge; but the core claim remains: at least some forms of self-awareness cannot be delusional.

## The wax argument and the inferential structure of perception

Descartes’ wax example is one of his most insightful arguments. There is a piece of wax before you, solid and with a definite shape. You put it on a warm pan. It loses its shape and becomes an amorphous puddle. Yet you know that the puddle is identical with the hexagonal solid object you saw ten minutes earlier.

Descartes’ point is that this knowledge cannot be purely perceptual. If you confined yourself to what the senses presently deliver, you would judge that the puddle is not identical with the earlier object, because their shapes differ. So your judgment of identity must involve an inferential or theoretical element. You tacitly rely on the principle that an object does not lose its identity merely because it changes in shape, temperature, or fragrance.

That principle is not itself given in perception. It is a precondition of your learning from perception at all. Without it, every change would appear to be obliteration followed by replacement by a numerically different object. But that is not how we take the world. We take ourselves to perceive one and the same object undergoing continuous change.

The lesson is twofold:

1. Beliefs about the external world are replete with **inferential** and **theoretical** content.
2. Because they involve such extrapolation, they are correspondingly precarious.

By contrast, knowledge that one is sad does not involve inference and so is not precarious in the same way. Thus self-knowledge is more secure than perceptual knowledge of the external world.

This fits Descartes’ **rationalism**. Not all knowledge is derived from the senses. Some knowledge is a precondition of perceptual knowledge. Conceptual truths such as “1 + 1 = 2,” and such claims as that triangles have three sides and that causes precede their effects, are not learned empirically.

## God and the attempted defeat of skepticism

Descartes does not think self-knowledge alone can justify our common-sense beliefs about the external world. To secure those beliefs he thinks it necessary to establish that God exists and is all-good, for only then can we trust that our cognitive faculties are generally reliable.

The argument of Meditation 3 proceeds through several steps.

First, Descartes invokes the principle that the cause of an event must have at least as much reality as the effect. The underlying thought is that something cannot come from nothing: no creation **ex nihilo**. Events and objects arise by redistribution of what already exists.

Second, he strengthens this into the claim that effects resemble their causes. The hotness of the pan resembles the hotness of the flame, and Descartes appears to generalize from this.

Third, he claims that each of us has concepts of infinity—of infinite goodness, infinite intelligence, and so on. From this he infers that infinite goodness and intelligence must somehow be “in” us.

From these premises he concludes that there must be an actually infinitely intelligent and good being: God.

The text is severe on this argument. The principle that something never comes from nothing is said to be reasonable enough. But the stronger resemblance claim is dubious, and the move from possessing an idea of infinity to containing infinity in some significant sense is where Descartes “goes totally wrong.”

Still, the structure matters. Descartes needs God for the next step. Once he thinks he has established that a good God exists, he argues as follows:

1. God is good.
2. A good God would not want us to be wrong all the time.
3. Therefore God has given us belief-forming mechanisms—senses and inferential capacities—that tend to generate a correct picture of the world.

This immediately raises a difficulty: why are we often wrong? Descartes’ answer appeals to **free will**. We err when we abuse freedom by drawing conclusions not warranted by the evidence. If we confine assent to what the evidence supports, we will have only correct beliefs.

This line of thought has both foundationalist and coherentist elements. But when Descartes tries to show that our perceptions must be caused by external objects resembling them, the argument depends on two premises the text rejects:

- that minds are completely transparent to themselves;
- that effects always resemble their causes.

The first is said to be unqualifiedly false. The second is false as stated, though perhaps salvageable as the weaker claim that effects tend to resemble their causes. The author even suggests that in this vicinity lies the adequate refutation of skepticism.

Meditation 5 adds a second proof of God, close to Anselm’s **ontological argument**:

1. God is maximally excellent by definition.
2. Anything deficient is not God.
3. Not existing is a deficiency.
4. Therefore God exists.

We are told flatly that this argument fails.

## Descartes’ dualism and the intensional fallacy

Meditation 6 is famous for its argument for **mind-body dualism**, the doctrine that mental entities are not identical with physical entities.

The argument runs roughly like this. Let x be a belief. Suppose I rightly believe x to be a belief. For any pattern of neural stimulation y, it does not follow that I believe y to be a belief. So x and y do not have the same properties, and therefore cannot be identical.

The standard objection is that this commits an **intensional fallacy**. Here we need the distinction between **intensional** and **extensional** contexts. An extensional context is one in which Leibniz’s Law applies without even apparent difficulty. An intensional context is one created by verbs like “believe,” “know,” and “doubt,” where substitution of co-referring expressions can appear to fail.

The stock example is Benjamin Franklin. The first postmaster general is the inventor of bifocals. Yet someone may believe that the first postmaster general is the first postmaster general without believing that the first postmaster general is the inventor of bifocals. This does not show that the first postmaster general is not the inventor of bifocals. It shows only that belief-contexts are intensional.

So too with Descartes. From the fact that I can believe that x is a belief without believing that x is a pattern of neural stimulation, it does not follow that beliefs are not patterns of neural stimulation.

The text makes the diagnosis more precise by distinguishing grammatical and logical complements. When Descartes says he can doubt the existence of a world made of matter, what he really means is that he can doubt **that** there exists a world made of matter. What differs in properties are propositions, not mind and matter themselves. Hence the original argument fails.

A refinement attempts to avoid this. One says:

1. I can coherently think: “x is a feeling, but x is not a brain-state.”
2. Therefore that statement is not analytically false.
3. All necessity is analytic.
4. So the statement is not necessarily false; it could be true.
5. Identity, if it holds at all, holds necessarily.
6. Therefore feelings are not brain-states.

This argument, too, is challenged. First, it can still be adapted to the intensional diagnosis. Second, many philosophers deny that all necessity is analytic. “Water is H2O,” for example, is said to be a necessary but non-analytic truth. This leads into a discussion of **natural kinds**, explanatorily and predictively fecund categories such as water, proton, acid, star, or penguin. On that widely accepted line, a thing’s microstructure may be essential to its natural kind even though it cannot be known a priori.

The text does not finally accept that broader picture, but it does proceed to what it treats as a compelling argument for dualism: Kripke’s.

## Kripke and the appearance-reality point about pain

Kripke’s argument exploits a difference between cases like water and cases like pain.

Take “water is H2O.” If this is a necessary but non-analytic truth, that is because something can appear just like water without being water, if it has the wrong microstructure. In general, non-analytic identity statements are possible where appearance can come apart from reality.

But pain is different. It makes no sense to say that something that felt just like a pain was not actually a pain. Anything that feels just like a pain is a pain. Therefore “pain is identical with brain state X,” if true, would have to be non-analytic; but the very feature that makes non-analytic necessities possible in other cases is absent here. So the identification fails.

This argument gains force from a broader claim developed later in the chapter: for at least some mental entities, especially appearances, the usual **appearance-reality dichotomy** seems inapplicable. If some mental entities are themselves appearances, then there may be no room to say that what seems to be present is merely an appearance masking some different underlying reality.

## The explanatory gap and the pressure toward materialism

The text then turns to the larger dispute between **dualism** and **materialism**. Materialism is the doctrine that mental entities are physical entities, typically brain-events or brain-structures. It is not **mental eliminativism**, which denies the existence of beliefs, pains, and so forth. Materialism says that these things exist, but are identical with physical states.

A central argument for dualism is the **explanatory gap**. We can discover **psychophysical concomitances**—truths of the form: mental phenomenon *m* occurs iff physical phenomenon *p* occurs. But this seems not to explain why the one is the other. If you shrank yourself to molecular size, you could in principle see H2O molecules and thereby grasp what is meant by “water is H2O.” If you shrank yourself and looked at a brain, you still would not see sadness, pain, or belief. Someone might know everything about the neural structure underlying pain and still not know what pain is; whereas someone ignorant of neurons may know exactly what pain is.

This is powerful, and the author regards the explanatory gap as real. Davidson’s argument for it is discussed but rejected because it depends on false assumptions, especially **interpretivism** and **functionalism**. Even so, the basic thought remains: mentalistic and physicalistic statements synthesize wholly different data. Even if they describe identical events, each leaves open whether the other is true.

Yet despite this, the author ultimately favors materialism. Why? Because of the causal argument.

The first and strongest argument is this:

1. Mental events obviously affect physical events, and physical events obviously affect mental events.
   - A hot iron touches your skin; you feel pain.
   - You intend to go to the store; you go to the store.
   - You feel nervous; your heart races.
2. There is extremely strong evidence that every physical event results only from other physical events.
3. Therefore either:
   - the mental has no effects on the physical, or
   - the mental is identical with the physical events that have those effects.
4. The first option is very hard to believe.
5. Therefore the second is correct: materialism.

This argument is endorsed as “pretty solid.” **Epiphenomenalism**, which says that the physical affects the mental but not vice versa, is rejected. Causation is said to be bidirectional: if my hand affects the table, the table affects my hand. Moreover, if mental events result from physical events and affect one another, then some energy associated with physical states must transfer to them; and unless that energy vanishes from the physical world never to return, mental events must be able to “spit it back” into the physical world.

A related materialist argument says that if mental entities are not physical, then non-physical items would be producing physical effects outside the scope of physical law. But there is no evidence of such violations, certainly not with anything like the frequency dualism would require.

Fodor’s argument compresses the point even further: the mental obviously affects the physical; anything that affects the physical is ipso facto physical itself. What is there to being physical other than the ability to displace mass-energy?

## Why behaviorism and functionalism fail

Among versions of materialism, the text discusses **behaviorism** and **functionalism**, rejecting both.

**Behaviorism** identifies mental states with dispositions to respond with overt behavior to sensory input. To believe that 1 + 1 = 2 is just to be disposed, when asked, to say “2.” The problem is obvious: such behavior depends on background mental states, such as knowledge of English. So mental states cannot be reduced to mere behavioral dispositions.

**Functionalism** is more sophisticated. For a state to be a belief that snow is white is for it to occupy the right **causal role**: to be caused by certain inputs and to cause certain outputs, including other mental states. This accommodates the dependence of behavior on internal mental organization.

But the text rejects functionalism decisively. First, for something to be a pain is for it to feel a certain way; its causal role is secondary. Second, the causal role of a pain is a consequence of its being pain, not what constitutes it. Third, functionalism threatens to define the mental in terms of itself, since the causes and effects of mental states include other mental states. The functionalist’s appeal to the **Ramsey sentence** is then criticized for making content too brittle: no two people have exactly the same causal role for any belief, so functionalism implausibly implies that no two people can share the same belief.

The deepest objection is this: it is states of affairs, not bare objects, that have causal powers. If functionalism identifies a belief with its having certain causes and effects, then that belief cannot itself be the cause of those effects. Cause and effect must be distinct. So functionalism deprives the mental of causal powers. Since the mental does have causal powers, functionalism is false.

## The unstable conclusion

The chapter ends in a state of productive tension. Materialism is probably correct, because mind and body interact and those interactions do not seem to involve violations of physical law. But two facts threaten materialism:

1. the mental seems different from the physical;
2. the appearance-reality dichotomy seems inapplicable to at least some mental entities, because some mental entities are appearances.

Taken together, these suggest that at least some apparent differences between mind and body are actual differences. That is why Descartes remains central even where he is mistaken. He forces philosophy to ask for rigorous justification, uncovers the peculiar security of certain forms of self-knowledge, reveals the inferential structure of ordinary perception, and frames with enduring sharpness the deepest problems about skepticism and the relation between mind and body.

title: Inference and Causal Anomalies
blurb: Hume’s challenge to induction is met by replacing uniformity with explanation’s minimization of causal anomalies.
body:
# Inference and Causal Anomalies

## Skepticism, doubt, and the scope of the problem

A **skeptic** is a doubter, not a disbeliever. That distinction matters from the outset. To be skeptical about Smith’s assertion that he is an astronaut is not to believe that he is not an astronaut; it is to doubt his claim. Skepticism is thus a withholding or questioning attitude. Yet skepticism has a tendency to slide into disbelief. If no positive evidence ever turns up for some claim, one naturally begins not merely to doubt it but to reject it. Sometimes that slide has a logical basis; sometimes it does not. The question here is when it does.

Philosophical skepticism concerns whole categories of putative truths. One may doubt truths affirming the existence of non-spatiotemporal entities, unconscious emotions, or theoretical entities. The two forms of skepticism at issue here are **skepticism about the external world** and **skepticism about inductive inference**.

Skepticism about the external world is doubt that our senses are telling us anything accurate. One who holds that there is no good reason to believe that sense-perceptions are anything more than hallucinations is a skeptic of this kind.

Skepticism about induction requires some preliminary distinctions. Some knowledge is **direct**: one simply knows it, without inference. A person in searing pain knows that he is in pain. But much knowledge is **indirect**: one has to figure it out. Indirect knowledge is acquired through **inference**. Every inference has **premises**—the beliefs or assumptions from which one reasons—and a **conclusion**—the belief one arrives at.

There are two kinds of inference:

1. **Deductive inference**: if the premises are true and the reasoning non-faulty, it is impossible for the conclusion to be false.
2. **Inductive inference**: if the premises are true and the reasoning non-faulty, it is still possible for the conclusion to be false.

If my premise is that x is a square and my conclusion is that x has four sides, the inference is deductive. If my premise is that in 35 years of drinking tap water I have never become sick from it, and my conclusion is that I will not become sick from the glass before me, the inference is inductive. The conclusion may be false.

A skeptic about induction holds that it is impossible, as a matter of principle, to learn anything through non-deductive inference. If that were right, then almost everything we take ourselves to know about the external world would collapse.

## Hume’s argument against induction

David Hume makes vivid why induction seems unjustifiable. His argument proceeds in a few steps.

### Step 1: Inductive inferences are not deductive

Consider: “The sun has always risen in the past; therefore, it will rise tomorrow.” This is not deductive. Even if the premise is true, it is not a theoretical impossibility that the conclusion be false. The sun might explode. So the conclusion is, at best, probable.

### Step 2: If not deductive, what warrants the inference?

Since the connection between premise and conclusion is not deductive, we must ask what reason the premise gives for accepting the conclusion.

The tempting answer is that the past resembles the future, the known resembles the unknown, nature is uniform. Call this the **uniformity principle** or **UP**. UP says, in effect, that because pinewood has floated, metal has expanded when heated, and water has quenched thirst up to now, we may rationally infer that they will continue to do so.

### Step 3: UP cannot justify induction without circularity

The difficulty is that UP is not directly known. At most, one directly knows only that certain regularities have held among the fragment of nature one has personally encountered. One does not directly know that they held among past objects unknown to one, nor that they will hold among future objects.

Any such knowledge would have to be inferential. But it cannot be deductive. From the fact that all ravens thus far known to me have been black, it does not deductively follow that ravens not yet known to me are black. So if UP is to be known at all, it must be known inductively. But then induction is being justified by appeal to a principle whose own warrant depends on induction. That is the circle.

Hence Hume’s conclusion: there is no way to justify inductive inference.

## Two alleged errors in Hume

The chapter’s strategy is to identify two serious mistakes in Hume’s argument.

1. Hume treats the primary form of non-deductive inference as **induction by enumeration**.
2. Hume assumes that non-deductive inference requires UP.

Both assumptions are rejected.

The more important form of non-deductive inference is **inference to the best explanation**. And the relevant principle is not UP but what is called **MC**, the principle of **minimization of causal anomalies**.

MC states: other things being equal, theory T1 is better than theory T2 if the world as T1 describes it contains fewer unexplained causal connections, fewer causal links that must simply be taken for granted and left unexplained.

The crucial claim is that MC, unlike UP, is **analytic**. That is, it is inherent in the very concept of explanation that, other things being equal, the better explanation is the one that eliminates more unexplained explainers, especially unexplained causal connections. Because MC is analytic, it need not be validated inductively. That is what is supposed to break Hume’s circle.

## Induction by enumeration and inference to the best explanation

An **induction by enumeration** has the form:

- Every F I have ever known of was also a G.
- Therefore, all F’s are G’s.

Example: all the balls I have thus far removed from the urn have been white; therefore all the balls in the urn are white.

An **inference to the best explanation** has a different form:

- It is known that S.
- It is not yet known that S*.
- But if S* were true, it would explain why S is true, without doing excessive violence to what we think we know about the world.
- Moreover, if S* were not true, it would be hard to find a viable alternative explanation of S.
- Therefore, we infer S*.

The example given is Larry and the unauthorized credit-card purchases. Before Larry moved in, no such purchases occurred. After he moved in, they did. The items purchased are ones Larry desperately needs and that almost nobody outside his unusual profession would want. In the absence of any other viable explanation, one concludes that Larry made the purchases.

The chapter’s central claim is strong: legitimate cases that are commonly described as induction by enumeration are really parasitic on inference to the best explanation. Straight enumerative induction, taken by itself, is spurious.

## The gambler’s fallacy and the worthlessness of bare enumeration

The argument against pure enumeration is sharpened by the example of roulette. You know the game is not rigged. The dice are not loaded. Nothing about you favors one outcome rather than another. You roll seven times, and each time at least one die lands in slot #27. It may feel natural to predict another 27. But that is irrational.

Why? Because, given the stipulated conditions, the next throw is no more likely to yield 27 than any other number. The same applies if you begin thinking the opposite—surely now 27 is less likely, because a long run of 27s is so improbable. That too is irrational. So long as the conditions are identical and nothing favors one result, no outcome is more or less likely than another. To suppose otherwise is, as the text says, the ultimate absurdity—like thinking that, although doughnut x is an atom-for-atom duplicate of doughnut y, x is far more fattening than y.

This is the **gambler’s fallacy**. The lesson is general. A run of phi’s that are psi’s gives one reason to expect the next phi to be psi only insofar as it gives one reason to believe in some underlying structure or mechanism that disposes phi’s to be psi’s. If one knows independently that there is no such mechanism, then no length of run provides a reason.

So the real structure of a non-fallacious inference is:

1. One knows of many phi’s that are psi’s and none that are not.
2. On that basis, one believes there is some principled connection between being a phi and being a psi.
3. Given that connection, if one encounters a new phi, one has reason to think it is likely to be a psi.
4. One concludes, tentatively, that it is a psi.

This is already inference to the best explanation. The mere concomitance does no work by itself. The work is done by the posited mechanism or law that would explain the concomitance.

## Hume’s reply and the need for a different principle

At this point Hume can respond: even if one posits a law or mechanism to explain why all known phi’s are psi’s, one still has no right to expect that law to continue unless one assumes nature is uniform. And if one assumes UP, the circularity returns.

That response is correct if UP is the needed principle. But the claim here is that in making an inductive inference one need not assume UP at all. One assumes only that explanations are supposed to eliminate causal anomalies. That is MC.

An **unexplained explainer** is something invoked to do explanatory work while itself being left unexplained. The purpose of explanation is to minimize the breadth and depth of what must simply be taken for granted. The more a theory forces one to say “things just happen that way; there is no explaining it,” the worse the theory is.

## The car theft case and explanatory cost

This is illustrated through the stolen car example. You park your car in front of your house, lock it, set the alarm, and put “The Club” on the steering wheel. You would almost certainly hear anyone approaching or tampering with the car. You hear nothing all night. Yet in the morning the car is gone.

Three explanations are considered:

- **E1**: A superhero-like creature used super powers to steal the car noiselessly.
- **E2**: The laws of physics changed overnight so that formerly noisy processes are no longer noisy.
- **E3**: Larry, your good friend with many auto-theft convictions and copies of your keys, stole the car.

E1 and E2 replace one mystery with far greater mysteries. E3 is not entirely innocent; it raises questions about your judgment of character and Larry’s apparent decency. Still, E3 is hands down the best explanation because it creates far fewer unexplained explainers than E1 or E2.

That is the operative notion of explanatory superiority. Not truth, not certainty, but minimization of causal anomalies.

## Good explanations need not be true

At this point the chapter introduces an important and striking distinction. A good explanation need not be the correct explanation.

The story of the smiling bus driver makes this vivid. The driver is smiling after a passenger gives him fifty $100 bills. One natural explanation is that he is pleased to have received a great deal of money. But Gus, who is unintelligent and completely insane, says the driver is a CIA assassin who that morning killed someone named Benjamin Franklin; seeing Franklin on the $100 bills reminded him of that enjoyable murder.

Gus’s explanation is absurdly bad relative to the data available. Yet, by stipulation, it turns out to be correct down to the last detail.

So explanatory goodness cannot be identified with truth. The chapter goes further. In the hypothetical world W*, we have exactly the same experiences as in the actual world, but the Gus-like explanations are always right. There, Santa Claus really is delivering gifts, stealthy gnomes really do take your keys, and so on. In W*, the good explanations, in the ordinary sense, are always wrong. Therefore there is no inherent connection between an explanation’s being good and its being true, or even likely to be true.

Explanatory goodness is a relation between explanation and data, not between explanation and reality. An explanation is good relative to a body of data when:

1. It is consistent with that data.
2. Among the competing explanations consistent with the data, it depends least on unexplained explainers.

That claim is central, and the chapter presents it as analytic.

## The plate on the table

The opaque plate case deepens the point. A plate is placed on a table, obscuring the part beneath it. Smith says it is a theoretical possibility that when the plate was placed there, a hole exactly the size of the plate came into existence in the table, while a special force appeared to keep the plate from falling.

Perhaps, in a bare logical sense, that story is coherent. It is not on a par with “squares are round.” But it is a terrible explanation. It generates question after question:

- Why did the hole appear?
- Why exactly that shape and size?
- Why did the force appear?
- Why was it perfectly calibrated?
- Why was there no independent evidence of it?

Every answer breeds more holes. The explanatory cost vastly exceeds the explanatory benefit.

Moreover, once one considers our entire belief system, it is not even clear that the deviant hypothesis is genuinely compatible with it. Suspending the natural laws needed to make the table chunk vanish would produce collateral damage. Suspending those effects would require second-order suspensions, which would in turn have further effects, and so on. The more one tries to save the deviant hypothesis, the more mutilated one’s belief system becomes. So even if a deviant hypothesis can be made logically consistent in some thin sense, its explanatory costs grossly outweigh its benefits.

## From limited law to generalization

Now the anti-Humean argument is assembled more carefully. Suppose Smith’s experience gives him reason to believe that, among metal objects within the scope of his past experience, being heated provides some kind of causal or **nomic** basis for expanding. Call that limited principle **P**. P applies only to past objects known to Smith.

At this stage, no question has been begged against Hume. One is not saying:

- that Smith’s experience entails a general law,
- or that it gives reason to think future metal will expand,
- or that it gives reason to think the law continues into the future.

One says only that Smith’s experience gives him reason to believe that such a connection has held within the domain of his experience.

Now suppose Smith accepts P. He faces two options:

1. Hold that P gives no reason at all to generalize beyond his past personal experience.
2. Hold that P warrants some generalization.

The most natural generalization is **P\***: the connection holds generally, for past and future objects alike, whether known by Smith or not.

What if Smith refuses any generalization? Then, given acceptance of P, he is implicitly committed to a bizarre world picture. Metal objects known to Smith would have to differ profoundly from those unknown to him; objects would undergo massive microstructural changes when they come within or pass beyond his awareness; laws would shift at the boundaries of his experience.

That is not conservative. It is wildly extravagant. It creates more unexplained explainers than the generalization does.

Likewise, if one says the law held in the past but will abruptly cease in the future, one is positing enormous discontinuities. Since the macroscopic supervenes on the microscopic, a change in whether heated metal expands would require innumerable microstructural changes. So abandoning the continuation of the law is not to posit one unexplained change but effectively innumerably many.

The supposedly cautious refusal to generalize is therefore not genuinely cautious. It embodies rejection of the analytic principle that explanations are to be preferred insofar as they create fewer unexplained explainers.

## The final structure of the reply to Hume

The argument closes in five steps.

1. **MC is analytic**: ceteris paribus, the better explanation is the one that creates fewer unexplained explainers.
2. It is a datum that various concomitances occur among objects known to us.
3. One creates more unexplained explainers by assuming that the unknown differs from the known than by assuming that it does not.
4. If one remains agnostic about whether the unknown resembles the known, one is committed to denying that there is reason to prefer explanations that explain more and burden us with fewer anomalies.
5. Therefore, given MC, there is an analytic and non-inductive reason to hold that, other things being equal, the unknown resembles the known.

That is the proposed answer to Hume. Hume is wrong because he thought the only route from known to unknown passed through UP. But the real route passes through explanatory practice itself, through MC.

## Skepticism about the external world

The same apparatus is then extended to skepticism about the external world. Sensory experience is full of discontinuities. Every time you open your eyes or turn your head, new experiences appear. The non-skeptic says these experiences do not come into existence ex nihilo; they are links in causal chains whose other links are unperceived. The skeptic says it is no more rational to believe this than to suppose that the experiences just arise from nowhere.

But that skeptical stance is extravagant in exactly the same way as the anti-generalizing stance in the induction case. It treats a theory that generates more causal anomalies as no worse than one that generates fewer. Since, on this conception, it is analytic that the theory with fewer anomalies is preferable, skepticism about the external world embodies an analytically false conception of explanation.

One must be careful here. It is not analytic that our sensory experiences are correct. But it is analytic that it is rational to suppose them veridical to the extent that doing so leaves us with fewer causal anomalies than the alternatives.

## A final qualification

There is, however, an important qualification in the chapter itself. The author states frankly that he is not fully convinced by the attempt to refute skepticism on this basis. He believes that the refutation of Hume’s analysis of inductive inference is cogent, and likewise the analysis of scientific explanation. What he does not believe to be cogent is the attempt to derive from that analysis a full refutation of skepticism.

That admission matters. It means the chapter’s strongest claims are not evenly distributed. The attack on **induction by enumeration** is forceful: it is assimilated to the gambler’s fallacy and treated as a bogus form of inference. The elevation of **inference to the best explanation** over enumerative induction is likewise central. And the account of explanation in terms of **minimization of causal anomalies** is presented as conceptually deep and analytically grounded.

Whether that suffices to defeat skepticism outright is left, by the author’s own lights, unsettled. But the conceptual shift it effects is clear. The issue is not whether we can somehow establish UP by induction. The issue is whether the very idea of explanation commits us to preferring continuity over arbitrary schism, lawful connection over brute anomaly, and worlds with fewer unexplained explainers over worlds with more. On that question, the chapter’s answer is unequivocal.

title: Empiricism and Its Limits
blurb: Why strict empiricism fails, why universals and non-empirical knowledge are unavoidable, and how Berkeley both erred and illuminated.
body:
# Empiricism and Its Limits

## Empiricism, rationalism, and the stakes

**Empiricism** is the doctrine that all knowledge is derived from **sense-perception**: sight, hearing, touch, and the like. **Rationalism** is the view that some knowledge is acquired entirely through reason. Rationalists need not deny that much knowledge comes through the senses; their claim is only that some knowledge does not. And, on the view presented here, that claim is correct.

The deepest issue is not whether the senses matter. They obviously do. The issue is whether they suffice. If every case of knowledge were strictly sense-based, then all justified true belief would have to be traceable, without remainder, to what perception gives us. The chapter’s thesis is that this is impossible. Strict empiricism is indefensible. Consequently, at least some knowledge has a non-perceptual basis.

A further metaphysical point immediately follows. Those who believe in **non-spatiotemporal** entities are necessarily rationalists. For empiricism is, nearly enough, the view that you do not know it if you do not see it. We see property-instances, but not properties themselves. Hence empiricists either deny properties themselves or identify them with spatiotemporal entities. Anyone who believes in uninstantiated properties, or in properties that are not spatiotemporal, is therefore a rationalist. **Platonists**, who hold that properties are non-spatiotemporal, are accordingly rationalists. A Platonic metaphysics requires a rationalist epistemology.

The chapter’s argumentative burden is thus substantial: to show that the mind’s commerce with the world presupposes non-empirical resources, and that empiricism, if consistently pursued, collapses either into skepticism or into Berkeleyan idealism.

## The particularity of perception and the need for universals

Sense-perception discloses only **particulars**: this object, here, now, with these property-instances. But understanding and explanation proceed through **universals**—also called **properties**, **categories**, natures, essences, or ways of being. These are exemplified by particulars but are not themselves sense-perceived.

Why are universals indispensable? Because explanation is impossible without them. Consider: “Why did Max steal the money? Because Max is greedy and amoral and he believed it to be to his strategic advantage to steal the money.” This explanation works only by citing characteristics under which Max falls and principles associated with those characteristics. It presupposes universals denoted by “greed,” “amorality,” “money,” and “theft.” And this is not an accidental feature of this one explanation. All explanations presuppose universals. The very idea of an explanation that did not do so is incoherent.

Now universals are outside space-time. Since causal relations hold only among spatiotemporal entities, universals cannot have causal effects. And one cannot sense-perceive an object without being affected by it. Therefore universals cannot be sense-perceived. Nor can one sense-perceive evidence of them, since **evidence** requires causal interconnection: smoke is evidence of fire because smoke and fire are causally connected in such a way that, given smoke, fire may reasonably be assumed. Hence there can be no observational basis for the existence of universals.

This yields a dilemma:

1. If empiricism is correct, we cannot have good reason to posit universals.
2. But thought, language, and explanation are saturated with universals.
3. Therefore the right move is to reject empiricism.

Empiricists sometimes respond by saying that instances of universals exist but universals per se do not. This fails for several reasons.

First, every sentence and every thought demands at least one universal.

Second, basic logic shows that universals exist. Consider: “Bob and Ted are both human; therefore, there is some characteristic that they have in common.” That inference is valid, and its conclusion affirms a universal.

Third, ordinary truths cannot be expressed without quantifying over properties. The sentences:

1. Hitler and Stalin had a lot in common;
2. Smith has what it takes to be a great pianist, but he doesn’t have what it takes to be a great composer;
3. Even though Smith is different from Jones, that has nothing to do with the fact that they don’t like each other

all have meanings that explicitly invoke properties. And they cannot be translated into statements that avoid such commitment.

Fourth, resemblance requires universals. For two objects to resemble one another in some respect just is for there to be some property that they both have. If two objects have the same shape in a world devoid of sentient beings, then that property exists in a world without thinkers. So properties are not created by thought and are not dependent on thinkers.

This also disposes of Locke’s claim that categories are “the workmanship of the understanding.” Since **categories** are identical with properties—x falls under a category iff x has a property—and properties exist independently of thought, so do categories. The chef or chemist or auto mechanic who groups glacial water with gasoline rather than with another pint of glacial water will be punished by reality. Why? Because his categories do not cut nature at the joints. Nature itself contains the relevant commonality.

## Perception presupposes non-perceptual cognition
