Second, the punitive character of many moral codes is compatible with the thesis. Left to himself, the individual behaves in ways that are radically anti-social. A non-restrictive, non-punitive moral code would fail to protect people from one another and so would fail in its purpose. Some excess punitiveness is also explicable by the fact that moral censure provides an outlet for aggression and antipathy that does not jeopardize social order.

At this stage a vital distinction appears: that a practice is immoral does not entail that others have the right to stop it. There are both moral and strategic reasons for tolerating divergent moral views. The author’s example is pointed: if we launch a wholesale invasion on a country so as to prevent its otherwise superb president from being mean to his children, we will do more harm than good. The invasion is immoral even if it prevents future mistreatment of those children. Similarly, since people cannot flourish without a certain amount of freedom, it is wrong to inhibit freedom except to prevent greater abridgments. Forced moral correction can itself be more immoral than the behavior it aims to stop.

## Moral principles as conditional truths

The chapter then withdraws even the earlier concession that moral truths do not pre-exist human beings. Moral principles may be understood as **conditional truths**. Let PBS name our psychological-biological structure. Then a moral principle has the form: if there were creatures with PBS, then treating them in certain ways would be wrong and treating them in certain other ways would be right.

This is why the claim that enslaving human beings was wrong even before there were people is not absurd. The principle is: if there are entities with PBS, they should not be enslaved. That statement can be true even when there are no such entities.

The relevant logical point is simple: **hypothetical truths** can hold whether or not their antecedents are true. Even if Smith has no money, it remains true that if Smith has a million dollars, then he has more than twenty dollars. Likewise, before there were people, the antecedent of “if there are people, they should not enslave one another” was false, but the conditional need not therefore be false.

To make this less mysterious, the chapter uses the example of Euclidean triangles. “Euclidean triangles have interior angles adding up to 180°” is, in effect, a universal statement about hypotheticals: if x is a Euclidean triangle, then its interior angles add up to 180°. Yet Euclidean triangles are physically impossible, since the structure of space prohibits them. If truths can concern entities that not only do not exist but could not physically exist, there is no reason to resist truths concerning humans in a person-free world, where humans are at any rate physically possible.

## Existence, knowledge, implementation

The decisive rebuttal to conventionalism turns on two distinctions:

1. The distinction between a moral law’s **existing** and its being **known**.
2. The distinction between a moral law’s being **known** and its being **implemented**.

Suppose there were a time when slavery was not felt to be wrong, and slaves themselves, damaged by their condition, accepted it as just. It does not follow that slavery was not wrong. One person’s brutalization of another is not made right by mutual acceptance of a spurious rationalization. Therefore a moral law can exist without being known.

From this the anti-conventionalist conclusion follows immediately: if we created moral laws, we would always know them. Since a moral law can exist without being known, we do not create moral laws.

And even when moral laws are known, they may not be implemented. Slave-owners may have known slavery was wrong while publicly denying it. They had powerful incentives to rationalize rather than confess. Openly admitting the evil of slavery would mobilize abolitionist forces and unsettle their own self-conception. It is often convenient to turn a blind eye to moral truths. Hence moral laws can be known without being implemented or explicitly endorsed.

This matters because conventions cannot fail to be implemented. It cannot be a convention that people wear green hats on Sunday unless people actually do so. Since moral laws can exist without implementation, they are not conventions.

## Argument #2: cultural relativism

The second argument appeals to intercultural variation. Some cultures accept polygamy, others do not. Either one culture must be wrong, or neither is right nor wrong. The first option is said to be implausible because differences in ethical outlook are likened to differences in taste, as when one person likes tennis and another prefers soccer. So the second option is embraced: where cultures diverge ethically, neither is right nor wrong. Therefore there are no moral facts.

The analysis proceeds in layers.

First, what people do in a culture does not show what they think is right. People knowingly do immoral things.

Second, what people officially say is right does not show what they really believe. They often lie, especially when a practice benefits them. A culture in which ownership of persons of a certain race or gender is officially legitimate need not be a culture whose members generally think the practice good. Those with power may sustain the practice by providing specious ethical rationalizations.

Third, apparent moral disagreement may mask agreement in value plus disagreement in factual belief. The example is child-beating. If people in culture X think beating children prevents them from becoming ineffective adults, whereas people in Y think beating is necessary to make them effective adults, then both may share the same value: one should help one’s children become effective adults. The practical divergence stems from different descriptive beliefs.

Even if there are real value differences, cultural relativism still does not follow. Consider the case where culture X tries to wipe out culture Y for no good reason: Y is no threat, invasion yields no benefit, and so on. What can the relativist say? If he says it is wrong, he concedes an intercultural standard and abandons relativism. If he says it is not wrong, he implies that nothing one culture does to another is wrong. Then obliterating a culture and its morality is permissible, and a culture’s morality is no more valid than its army is powerful. **Might makes right.** But that conclusion destroys the very sentiment of tolerance that supposedly motivates cultural relativism. Therefore cultural relativism is **self-defeating**.

Again the chapter insists on a distinction often blurred: “What they do in culture X is wrong” does not imply “we have the right to stop them.” The Dictator of Country X may beat his wife. That is immoral. Still, invading X to prevent this may unleash murders, rapes, and general disorder far worse than the original evil. Interventions undermine regularity-conducive structures such as governments and stable institutions, which are precisely what make prediction possible. Since intervention is justified only when there is a reasonable expectation that the post-intervention situation will be better, and since such expectation is often impossible when institutions are destabilized, intervention is often unjustified.

Autonomy is also central. No person and no nation would have much freedom if not allowed, within limits, to do wrong. Therefore one can have an obligation to refrain from preventing acts one knows to be wrong. This shows the spuriousness of the inference from “it is wrong” to “we may stop it.”

## Argument #3: science has no use for moral facts

The third argument says that no exhaustive scientific description of the world would mention wickedness or decency. Science speaks of atoms, protons, positive and negative charges, not of right and wrong. Therefore we have no reason to posit moral facts.

The reply is conditional but forceful: if ethical facts are natural facts, science must countenance them. On **utilitarianism**, an act is good insofar as it promotes happiness and bad insofar as it promotes unhappiness. On **virtue theory**, an act is good insofar as it promotes the development of inborn potential and bad insofar as it prevents it. Science certainly does not deny that acts differ in their tendency to produce happiness or to encourage the development of inborn potential. So, if these theories are correct, moral facts fall within natural science.

The confusion behind the anti-moral argument is a semantic one. It assumes that if two sentences register the same fact, they must be synonymous. That is false. “Smith has two cars” can register the same fact as “if n is a number such that n = 2 iff arithmetic is incomplete and such that n = 3 otherwise, it follows that Smith has n cars.” The sentences are not synonymous, yet they concern the same fact. So even if moral vocabulary picks out facts also describable in physical, biological, or psychological terms, it does not follow that moral statements are meaningless or scientifically illicit.

## Argument #4: ethical statements say only “should”

The fourth argument begins with a linguistic claim: “abortion is morally wrong” means “abortions should not occur”; “keeping promises is morally right” means “promises should be kept.” Ethical statements say what should be, not what is. But reality is described by saying what is the case, not what should be the case. Hence the normative component adds nothing factual. “Smith was wrong to kill Jones” says nothing beyond “Smith killed Jones.” Therefore ethical utterances are not true or false statements but **pseudo-statements**.

The response is to reconceive moral imperatives as **hypothetical imperatives**. A hypothetical imperative has the form: given that you want x, you should do y. These are perfectly ordinary, causal claims and fall within natural science.

One cannot give an amoral person any good reason to be moral, precisely as moral. Any reason one has to be moral is hypothetical:

1. Given that your objective is to be moral, you should do X.

Different theories specify X differently. Under utilitarianism:

2. Given that your objective is to maximize happiness, you should do X.

But this amounts to a causal statement:

3. Not doing X will have the consequence that people are not as happy as they would otherwise be.

This is parallel to engineering:

4. Given that your objective is to construct a sturdy bridge, you should use material X.

which means:

5. Not using material X will have the consequence that the bridge is not as sturdy as it would otherwise be.

Thus the “shoulds” of ethics are like the “shoulds” of engineering. Under practically any ethical theory, if the theory is correct, its imperatives become causal statements concerning how certain ends are or are not realized.

## Argument #5: ethical judgment necessarily motivates

The fifth argument attributes a special property to ethical statements: if understood and believed true, they necessarily incline one toward certain actions. If you truly understand and accept that you should keep promises, you must be inclined to keep them. Descriptive statements lack this feature. Hence ethical statements are not descriptive and say nothing.

The reply denies both crucial premises.

First, ethical statements do not necessarily incline those who agree with them to act accordingly. Many people do what they know is ethically wrong and have not the slightest inclination not to do it. Often the very wrongness of the act contributes to its appeal. The suggestion that every norm-violator is moved, consciously or unconsciously, by a countervailing inclination toward compliance lacks empirical support. And psychologically it is implausible. People do not wish to suppress awareness of noble impulses; they wish to suppress awareness of ugly and evil ones. So it is the ignoble motives that are more likely to disappear into the unconscious.

The chapter’s psychological picture is severe: the wrong path is the easy path. Unethical acts are acts of giving in. A person’s default mode is to act unethically. “Absolute power corrupts absolutely,” as Lord Acton said. When people do not have to act morally, they do not, because they do not want to. Hence it is false that grasp of an ethical principle automatically produces reluctance to violate it. The ethical is what you do not want to do.

Second, insofar as ethical statements do motivate, they do so only through accompanying descriptive beliefs. You feel compelled to give money to charity X only insofar as you believe doing so will alleviate hunger or produce some other effect. Knowledge of moral truth moves action only to the extent that it coincides with knowledge of descriptive truth. So if moral understanding motivates, that supports rather than undermines the claim that moral truths coincide with descriptive truths.

## Argument #6: ethics as propaganda

The sixth argument says ethical statements are instruments of propaganda. The examples are political: in Hitler’s Germany, obeying the Führer was “good”; in Stalin’s Russia, questioning the Communist Party was treachery; in capitalist countries, regulation of private property is described as a gross violation of fundamental human rights even when needed for basic services, while further enrichment of the already rich is treated as unobjectionable though it impoverishes others. Ethical codes, on this view, manipulate the have-nots into serving the haves by misrepresenting injustice as justice.

The reply is direct. Not everything everyone describes as moral is moral. The Nazis were wrong, and most of them knew it. So the fact that claims about morality are often propaganda does not show that morality itself is propaganda.

Moreover, legitimate moral principles can be put to evil use. If a police officer bludgeons someone to death for speeding and justifies it by saying speeding must be punished to keep highways safe, he is exploiting a good moral principle—people should not speed or otherwise endanger others—for an evil purpose. Evil regimes routinely seek legitimate moral underpinnings for nefarious policies. That moral language can be abused does not show that moral truth is itself abusive illusion.

## The overall position

The chapter’s cumulative view is clear. Morality is neither convention nor pseudo-statement nor mere intercultural preference nor manipulative propaganda. Moral truths are grounded in facts about beings with our PBS: facts about damage, flourishing, freedom, and the social conditions under which creatures like us can live well together. These truths may be unknown, denied, unapplied, or cynically exploited. Their existence is not threatened by any of that. Indeed, the distinction between existence, knowledge, and implementation is indispensable if one is to make sense of slavery, Nazism, Stalinism, and the ordinary human propensity to rationalize what one knows to be wrong.

The chapter therefore rejects both **moral conventionalism** and **moral nihilism**. Against conventionalism, morality is not made true by endorsement or practice. Against nihilism, moral claims are not empty. They are anchored in the descriptive reality of what beings like us are and what helps or harms us.

title: Subjecthood, Flourishing, Morality
blurb: A defense of the qualified claim that morality is tied to self-interest through subjecthood, flourishing, and conscience.
body:
# Subjecthood, Flourishing, Morality

## Practical and categorical incentives

There are often pragmatic incentives to act morally. One avoids jail, preserves a career, curries favor with institutions, and secures cooperation from others. But the central question is not whether morality is often prudentially useful. It is whether morality is **categorically** in one’s interest: whether, setting aside merely situational advantages, there is a deeper connection between morality and one’s own welfare.

The answer defended here is a very qualified yes. The qualification matters because, on the surface, it is often to one’s advantage to be immoral.

The laws we create are meant to incentivize moral conduct and dis-incentivize immoral conduct. Since murder, assault, rape, theft, and extortion are punished, the legally available forms of pursuit tend to involve behavior that is at least somewhat conducive to others’ welfare. Yet no viable legal system could possibly dis-incentivize all immorality. Laws are blunt instruments, and they should be. A legal order that eliminated every form of immorality would also eliminate nearly every form of aggressive, anti-social, and self-interested conduct except in the relatively few cases where it benefits others.

The result would be disastrous. There would be no Beethovens, no Einsteins, no Freuds, no Mendelssohns, no Emily Dickinsons, no Madame Curies, and no Emily Brontes. There would be no geniuses, no conquerors—only bureaucrats. The point is not that great accomplishment is simply evil; it is that, more often than not, some aggression and narcissism underlies it. A world of completely moral people, in the ordinary sense, would contain no innovators, no creators, only milquetoast do-gooders and innocuous squares. Since preventing flourishing is itself profoundly evil, a legal system that made all immorality impossible would be supremely immoral. It would also annihilate autonomy: if acting immorally were not even an option, one would have no options.

So the connection between morality and self-interest is not straightforward. In some circumstances it is to one’s advantage to act morally; in others it is not. Indeed, many people would be happier if they were less moral, because excessive morality can turn a person into a weakling or conformist whose every action depends on the approval of others.

## Moral worth and Brown the sadist

A deeper complication follows. Suppose one behaves ethically only because it is advantageous. Then, so far as one’s reason is self-advantage, one’s behavior has no **moral worth**.

This is brought out by Brown, the sadist and serial killer. Brown is drafted into the military during wartime and serves as interrogator, torturer, and executioner. As it happens, his country is a liberal, tolerant, peaceful democracy defending itself against a barbaric totalitarian invader. Brown’s job performance therefore has very positive consequences for humanity. Yet Brown’s conduct is fueled by hate and ill-will, not by any love of justice. He wants to hurt people; if he discovered that his actions improved the human condition, he would enjoy his work less, and if he discovered that they worsened it, he would enjoy it more.

Brown’s overt behavior coincides with that of somebody acting ethically. But his motives drain it of moral worth. The general claim is:

1. For behavior to be **moral**, the agent’s intention must be to do the right thing.
2. External behavioral coincidence is not enough.
3. Therefore conduct can be behaviorally indistinguishable from moral conduct and yet not itself be moral.

This establishes that mere prudential alignment with moral requirements is not morality properly speaking.

## Hyper-morality and self-hate

The ordinary conception of morality also often militates against happiness. Publicly accepted systems of morality typically hold that, with a few exceptions, no act advantageous to oneself is permissible if it hurts someone else. The deeply moral person therefore often grossly undervalues his own needs and aspirations.

There is also a deeper connection between **hyper-morality** and unhappiness. Hyper-morality requires a punitive conscience: a conscience that permits one to do, feel, or think as one wishes only under narrow conditions. Such a conscience holds one’s own psychological needs in contempt. It embodies hate, contempt, and aggression toward a facet of oneself. Thus the essence of hyper-morality is a kind of self-hate. Since nobody weighed down by such a conscience can be fully happy, perfect morality is neither necessary nor sufficient for happiness.

And some immoral people are authentically happy. Not merely pleasantly stimulated, not self-deceived, but integratedly happy.

That should not tempt us into the shallow judgment that morality has nothing to do with happiness. The relation is deeper than the ordinary morality of self-sacrifice suggests.

## Happiness as value-laden structure

**Happiness** is not simply a feeling. It consists, at least partly, in judging that one’s life conforms to some ideal one has and therefore complies with some value. Happiness is a conviction that how one is coincides with how, relative to some value system, one should be. It is therefore partly a moral concept.

Consider the ice-cream example. You have a flabby physique. You can go for a jog or eat a bucket of ice cream. You eat the ice cream and then feel ashamed. The shame shows that, in your own eyes, you have done something wrong: you have fallen short of an ideal, failed to live up to your values, and are unhappy vis-à-vis this situation. Modify the story: you go for the jog instead. You are proud of yourself and delighted that you are closer to your objective. You are happy vis-à-vis this situation.

So:

1. Happiness and unhappiness apply only where there are values.
2. Anything that values anything has a value system and thus a morality.
3. To be happy, a creature must not merely have values but live up to certain ones it has.

This does not mean one must satisfy every value one countenances. A non-sociopathic person sincerely countenances many values that cannot all be fully complied with. But happiness, as distinct from mere pleasantness, requires living up to some values one has.

## Necessary and sufficient conditions

Is it enough, for happiness, to live up to one’s values? Yes—but one’s values concern not only action but also one’s condition.

Smith is a great novelist who has fully capitalized on his talent, but he has a terrible chronic illness causing constant pain. Is he happy? No. This does not refute the analysis. He wants to be healthy and pain-free, but he is neither. His actual self therefore fails to align with his idealized self. It is irrelevant that the failure is not his fault.

Happiness thus includes the conviction that one is as one wants oneself to be. Since one may want health, freedom from pain, artistic achievement, familial harmony, and so on, one can be happy in some respects and unhappy in others.

This leads to a crucial distinction: happiness is a **structure**, not a feeling. Beliefs, values, and personality traits are structures. Joy and pleasure are passing states—**structure-internal events**. Happiness is like knowledge that 1 + 1 = 2, not like a transient feeling of joy. It gives rise to joy and pleasure, but is not identical with them.

That is why it makes sense to say that Smith may be happy vis-à-vis his work but unhappy vis-à-vis his health. A positive value-judgment about oneself tends to generate pleasant feelings; a negative one unpleasant feelings. But the judgment is not the feeling.

## Subjecthood and the prerequisites of happiness

There is happiness only where there is an enduring **subject**; a mere body is not enough. There is an enduring subject only where there is a certain degree of **self-consciousness**. And, following Harry Frankfurt, there is personhood where there is an alignment of higher-order desires with lower-order desires.

The chapter’s deeper claim is that **norm-drivenness** is constitutive of subjecthood. A mental event is norm-driven when it responds to another mental event in light of what, given the content of that other event, ought to follow. A **value-driven** act is one driven by a wish to make reality conform to some value.

The argument begins with X, a creature of one-thousandth your intelligence whose life is one ecstasy after another. X enjoys one-dimensional pleasures, but does not synthesize experiences, define objectives, or want anything. Everything is handed to it. It merely feels, and feels good—ecstatically. But X is neither happy nor unhappy; the concept of happiness is inapplicable.

Why? Because there is no clear subject there. There are mental states, perhaps, but not a single mind to which they belong. Contrast this with “Joe Biden” or “Fido,” which refer not merely to bodies but to embodied presences, persons or animal personalities. X seems unlike that. Its mental episodes merely occur in a body.

## Why causation is not enough

The crucial defense proceeds through the Max examples. Suppose at time t you learn that Max has exactly four cars. Let this belief be M1. At time t* you come to believe that Max has more than two cars. Let that belief be M2.

Now distinguish:

- one belief’s causing another;
- one believing’s leading to another believing.

If M1 brings about M2 because of some irrelevant physical feature of the brain-state underlying M1—say, its shape causes a migraine that induces hallucinations of Max showing titles to three cars—then your belief that Max has four cars caused your belief that Max has more than two cars. But your **believing** that Max has four cars had nothing to do with your **believing** that he has more than two cars. The content was irrelevant.

By contrast, if you validly infer from “Max has four cars” to “Max has more than two cars,” then your believing the former leads to your believing the latter in a content-sensitive way. The transition is guided by what ought to be believed, given the content of the first belief. That is a norm-driven response.

The same applies to practical and emotional life. If I find cow brain repellant, I avoid eating it again and avoid situations likely to involve eating it. This is not a brute sequence. It is guided by an understanding of what I should do given what I want and believe.

Hence:

1. Mental states form a single mind only if some of them are **content-driven responses** to others.
2. Content-driven responses are norm-driven responses.
3. Norm-driven responses require self-consciousness, because one mental event must embody awareness of another’s content and of what is appropriate given it.
4. Therefore norm-drivenness is constitutive of subjecthood.

A mere sequence of mental events, even causally connected, is not yet a subject.

## Animals, value, and proto-morality

This account rejects the narrow claim that only human beings are self-conscious or have values. Cats and dogs plainly have cumulative mental lives. They learn, develop attitudes, have desires, perhaps even objectives. Their experiences are not isolated episodes. So they have the kind of self-consciousness needed for subjecthood, even if they lack the more abstract form humans possess.

Because subjecthood requires normatively cohesive mental life, and normativity is sensitivity to what ought to be the case, value is built into subjecthood itself. The essence of subjecthood is sensitivity to value and therefore to a kind of **proto-morality**, if not full-fledged morality.

So morality has much deeper roots than commonly thought. It lies at the foundation of subjecthood.

## Morality as respect for subjects

Now the thesis sharpens. **Morality** is respect for subjects qua subjects. Moral values are those that must be complied with if subjects are to be allowed to exist—if multiplicities of mental states are to maintain the integrity required to constitute single minds.

This allows the transition to the central evaluative claim: the one thing with **non-derivative moral value** is **flourishing**.

Smith, talented at writing novels, suppresses his vocation because he believes morality requires serving the needy. He installs sewage systems, feeds the hungry, and lives in misery. Brown, by contrast, is a selfish swine who writes novels, develops his talent, listens carefully to criticism, and flourishes. Brown’s life is richer, better, less empty. Smith’s is morally better in the ordinary altruistic sense, but not better in the sense relevant to his own welfare.

What follows is severe: a life of self-effacement is built around the premise that one’s own life is worthless. Any ethical system that requires suppression of the true self is evil and incoherent. If a person’s true self contains evil elements, a viable ethical system should redirect them relatively harmlessly, not demand self-mutilation.

Flourishing is not self-indulgence. Brown is self-disciplined: he forgoes narcotics and debauchery because they would weaken his artistic ability. Smith is self-disciplined too, but in a self-torturing way that denies who he is. The distinction is between self-discipline in the service of flourishing and self-denial that extirpates the self.

## Duty and aspiration

This yields the distinction between the **morality of duty** and the **morality of aspiration**.

- The morality of duty consists of the familiar prohibitions against killing, stealing, lying, and so on.
- The morality of aspiration consists of the directives one must follow to have a genuinely good life, the kind of life Brown has rather than Smith.

The chapter insists that the morality of aspiration really is morality, because flourishing has intrinsic moral value. To say otherwise would be absurd. The claim

> It is morally valuable to help others flourish; but a person’s flourishing does not itself have moral worth

is compared to saying that effective medicines have value because they produce good health, but good health has no value. Nonsense. If helping others flourish is morally valuable, that value must derive from flourishing itself.

## Why duty matters, and why it may not bind the flourishing individual

The morality of duty matters because flourishing depends on social institutions. Our aspirations—to be judges, engineers, novelists, physicians, philosophers—presuppose social infrastructure. More deeply, they derive their meaning from social forms of life. In a war of all against all, novel writing would be like designing tea-cozies in the middle of a battle: perhaps meaningful in content, but meaningless as an activity there.

Even narcissistic creators address an audience—actual, future, or imagined. Beethoven was not talking only to himself. Gianni Versace’s designs were meaningful responses to existing style. Human flourishing is therefore not merely causally dependent on cooperative social arrangements; it is logically tethered to them.

So the morality of aspiration depends on the morality of duty. But crucially, it does not follow that *one oneself* must comply with the morality of duty in order to flourish. Brown can flourish in a world where others preserve the institutions on which his novel writing depends. Compliance with duty is necessary somewhere in the system, but not necessarily by the flourishing individual. This is why the connection between morality and self-interest is qualified.

## Conscience, self-censure, and non-trivial success

The final deep connection appears in **conscience**. A person with no conscience rationalizes failure, never taking responsibility and thus never making needed corrections. For that reason, people of no conscience—**psychopaths** or **sociopaths**, used interchangeably here—are dismal failures in life. Psychopathy is not psychosis: it is not a break with reality but the absence, or near-absence, of conscience.

Being evil is not the same as being a psychopath. Evil people can have consciences. Roy DeMeo, a Mafia Capo and killer, was evil; yet by his son’s account he was a good father and husband, and even professionally he honored contracts and repaid debts. That was partly prudential, but probably also partly professional pride.

The key contrast is between psychopaths and evil non-psychopaths such as Mao. The psychopath rationalizes failure. The evil non-psychopath self-censures when he falls short of his own standards. Mao had to ask himself whether he was doing what he had to do to achieve his ends; if not, he had to change himself. This attitude is captured by the formulation labeled **MM**:

> There are standards. I can fall short of them, just like anyone else. And I have fallen short of them... I must blame myself... and change myself so that I don’t repeat it.

That structure of self-censure embodies a morality of duty. In censuring oneself, one takes oneself to be just another person accountable to standards larger than oneself. This is the essence of duty.

Hence:

1. Any non-trivial flourishing requires self-censure and self-correction.
2. Self-censure embodies a morality of duty.
3. Therefore some morality of duty is inherent in any case of non-trivial flourishing.

Psychopaths can perform small cons, manipulate, swindle, even kill. But because they do not genuinely hold themselves to standards, they do not achieve large-scale success. History’s great villains tend not to be psychopaths. They are evil non-psychopaths with enough conscience to discipline themselves.

## Flourishing as the moral constant

Differences in moral outlook do not undermine this analysis. People and cultures disagree, not about whether flourishing is good, but about what flourishing consists in. One person may identify it with keen intellect, another with wealth, another with power, another with loyalty to country, another with doing God’s will, another with kindness. The disagreement is over the content of flourishing, not over its value.

No one thinks flourishing is bad or that its frustration is good. Thus the underlying moral agreement is deeper than apparent disagreement suggests.

The conclusion is therefore twofold. First, morality in the ordinary sense is not always in one’s interest, and excessive morality may destroy happiness. Second, morality in a deeper sense—value, norm-drivenness, flourishing, conscience—is constitutive of subjecthood itself and indispensable to any serious human success. That is why the answer to whether it is categorically in one’s interest to act morally is a qualified yes. The morality that is categorically tied to self-interest is not primarily the morality of self-sacrifice, but the morality embedded in subjecthood, aspiration, flourishing, and the self-corrective discipline of conscience.

title: Rationality, Autonomy, and Kant
blurb: A critical reconstruction of Kant’s ethics, its failures, and its enduring insight into autonomy and rationality.
body:
# Rationality, Autonomy, and Kant

## Kant’s project and its problem

Kant is presented here as both a great epistemologist and a great ethicist whose ethical insights are entangled with serious confusion. The central issue is his attempt to identify morality with self-interest. The author agrees with Kant on one broad thesis: it is categorically in one’s interest to act ethically. But Kant’s understanding of morality differs sharply from the conception the author accepts, and this difference matters because Kant’s route from morality to self-interest therefore goes astray.

Kant is said to offer **two theories of morality**.

1. According to the first, an act is moral just in case, were everyone else to act similarly, that act would not be self-defeating.
2. According to the second, an act is moral to the extent that it embodies respect for people’s **autonomy**.

**Autonomy** means self-determination: for a person to be autonomous is for him, not someone else, to decide how he will live. Its opposite is **heteronomy**. Someone is heteronomous to the extent that others decide how he lives. So, on the second theory, autonomy-conducive acts are good and heteronomy-conducive acts are bad.

Kant thinks these two formulations are equivalent. The chapter’s governing claim is that they are not equivalent, and that his failure to distinguish them ruins his specific attempt to connect morality with self-interest.

## Categorical imperatives and three distinct questions

A **categorical imperative** is a rule one should follow no matter what: “imperative” means command or rule, and “categorical” means unconditional. But the question “Are there any categorical imperatives?” is ambiguous. It may ask:

1. Are there any moral rules that one simply should follow?
2. Are there any rules of any kind at all that one simply should follow?
3. Are there any moral rules that hold without exception? That is, supposing one’s intention is to be moral, are there any moral rules one must follow under any circumstances?

The answer to the first two questions is said to be no.

The reason is that statements of the form “one should refrain from committing immoral acts” are ambiguous between:

- “one should act morally if one’s objective is to act morally,” and
- “one should act morally, even if it is in one’s interest not to do so.”

The first is only a **hypothetical imperative** and is vacuous. The second is false. In general, what one should do depends on what one’s intentions are. Hence there are no moral rules one simply should follow in that sense; and the same reasoning defeats the more general claim that there are rules of any kind one simply should follow.

But the third question receives a yes. There are **categorical moral obligations** in the sense that certain moral principles hold without exception. One has a categorical moral obligation not to obliterate all life, and one has a categorical moral obligation to act morally. Kant, however, wants more: he wants non-trivial categorical moral imperatives. The chapter attributes to him these two:

1. **CI1**: An act is moral if it would not be self-defeating were everyone else to act similarly.
2. **CI2**: An act is wrong if it treats a person as an object rather than a subject, and right if it treats a person as a subject rather than an object.

CI2 is the autonomy formulation: always treat people as subjects, never as objects.

## Why CI1 and CI2 are not equivalent

The intuitive case for equivalence is easy to see. In a world where everyone lies, lying becomes pointless because nobody believes anyone. In a world where everyone steals, theft becomes pointless because everyone protects his possessions. So one might think that what is wrong with lying and stealing is precisely that they collapse when universalized; and one might then identify this with using people as objects.

But the chapter insists this is mistaken.

### First argument: bad acts need not be self-defeating when universalized

Consider a world of con-men. Kant’s thought would be: if everyone is constantly trying to con everyone else, everyone is so guarded that no one can successfully con anyone. But this is too quick. In a world of con-men, the smart con-men could con the not so smart con-men. So there are morally bad acts—acts of con-artistry—that would not necessarily be self-defeating in a world where everyone acted that way.

This yields two conclusions:

1. **CI1 and CI2 are not equivalent**, because people could still use people in a world where everybody was a user.
2. **CI1 is false**, because some plainly immoral acts would still succeed even if universalized.

### Second argument: good acts can fail when universalized

Now move in the opposite direction. There are morally good forms of conduct that could not be successfully carried out if universalized. Physicians heal people, and healing people is good. Yet nobody could successfully practice medicine in a world of physicians. Who would grow crops, build roads, enforce the law, and so on? So universalizability in the self-defeating sense is not sufficient for moral goodness and not necessary for it either.

That is the basic demolition of CI1.

## The deeper fallacy: categorical obligation is not exceptionlessness in action

The chapter’s most important correction to Kant appears in the story about stealing from Smith.

You are friends with Smith. Smith has money; you do not. Your children need medication immediately or they will die. Smith is well-meaning and does not want your children to die, but for some reason it is impossible for him to lend you the money. The only way to get it is to steal it. You have exactly two choices:

1. Steal from Smith.
2. Let your children die.

You steal. Your children live, and Smith is bankrupt.

The author says this is obviously the right thing to do. Lost money can be regained. Lost life cannot. But crucially, this does **not** show that stealing is not categorically wrong. It shows that stealing here is the **lesser of two evils**.

That distinction is decisive. A moral principle can hold categorically without dictating action in every case, because categorical obligations can conflict and can differ in weight. In this case:

- You have a categorical obligation not to steal.
- You have a stronger categorical obligation not to let your children die.

The second outweighs the first. But the first does not cease to exist.

This is supported by the phenomenon of remorse. If, under these circumstances, you ceased to have any obligation not to steal from Smith, then any remorse you felt would have no objective basis; it would be the emotional counterpart of a hallucination. But it would be monstrous to feel no remorse at bankrupting Smith, even though it would have been far more monstrous to let your children die. The fittingness of remorse shows that the obligation not to steal survives; it is merely outweighed.

The same structure applies elsewhere:

- Lying, cheating, stealing, manipulating, wounding are categorically bad.
- Yet they can sometimes be the lesser of two evils.
- Torture is wrong, but it is more wrong to allow a nuclear device to be detonated in the middle of a city.

So the right revision is not Kant’s absolute ban, but this more nuanced principle:

- It is categorically wrong to treat people as objects, but there are circumstances where that obligation is outweighed by some other obligation, for example the obligation not to allow ten million people to die.

The chapter labels this revised autonomy principle **CI2\***.

## Kant’s binary conception of morality

Why did Kant miss this? The chapter says he treated moral laws as if they were like legal statutes.

A legal statute does not have a **dimension of weight**. Legality is binary: an act is either legal or illegal. Of course laws can contain exception clauses, but given the law as stated, one either violates it or one does not.

Moral principles are different. Ronald Dworkin’s point is invoked here: moral principles have a dimension of weight. They can all remain in force while varying in relevance and comparative importance. The example is ordinary: I have a professional and ethical responsibility to teach class on Tuesday; I also promised a friend I would meet him for lunch, and I cannot contact him to cancel. The obligation to teach outweighs the obligation to keep the lunch-date. But the latter obligation still exists. That is why standing my friend up is a morally substandard thing to do even when justified all things considered.

Kant’s mistake is to have modeled morality on legality. He assumed that if a moral law does not determine action in a case, then it does not hold in that case. The chapter’s view is the opposite: moral laws can hold categorically and still be overridden.

## The good and the praiseworthy

A further Kantian blunder is failure to distinguish the **good** from the **praiseworthy**. Kant held that nothing other than a **good will** has any moral value. A good will is an intention to follow the moral law, and for Kant the moral law is CI2.

His reasoning runs as follows:

1. An intention to do good cannot itself be bad.
2. Anything else—intelligence, self-control, wealth, health—can be bad if possessed by a villain.
3. Therefore only the intention to do good has inherent moral worth.

The chapter grants the first step but denies the conclusion.

The counterexample is Brown, a happy two-year-old infant. Brown did not work for his happiness; he just happens to be happy.

- Does Brown’s happiness have moral value? Yes, obviously. That is why it would be wrong to make Brown unhappy.
- Does Brown deserve praise for being happy? No.

So some things are morally good without being commendable. Kant confuses the morally good with the praiseworthy or deserving of praise.

Another objection cuts deeper. Kant’s view is self-undermining. If it is inherently good to intend to respect autonomy, then autonomy itself must be inherently good. It would make no sense to say:

1. autonomy is not inherently good, but
2. an intention to respect autonomy is inherently good.

If the intention derives its worth from autonomy, autonomy must itself be good. So Kant cannot consistently maintain that nothing is inherently good except the intention to respect autonomy. Moreover, the intelligence of a villain is, the chapter says, indistinguishable from his autonomy: take away his intellect, and you take away much of his autonomy, if not all of it. Intelligence therefore looks inherently good even in the villain, though it may be outweighed by greater goods in certain circumstances.

The example of lobotomizing a villain makes the point. If a villain’s intelligence guarantees that he will kill millions unless lobotomized, then lobotomizing him may be the lesser of two evils. But that does not show his intelligence lacked inherent goodness. It shows only that one inherent good can be outweighed by another, greater inherent good.

## Kant’s argument linking morality and self-interest

Kant’s own argument for the coalescence of morality and self-interest is then stated.

1. We have value to the extent that we are rational.
2. So far as we subvert our rationality, we undermine ourselves.
3. Given an immoral act, the very idea of a world in which everyone committed that act is incoherent.
4. Therefore immoral acts are themselves incoherent, and hence irrational.
5. Since irrationality is self-undermining, immorality is self-undermining.
6. Therefore it is inherently in one’s interest to be moral.

The flaw is a massive non-sequitur. From the claim that a world in which everyone lies and still benefits from lying is incoherent, Kant infers that my lying here and now is incoherent. But whether an act is rational depends on the actual situation, not on some different situation. In our world, my lying does not entail that everyone lies, nor is it necessarily self-defeating for some other reason. So the move from universal incoherence to local irrationality does not go through.

## Universalizable: the equivocation

Why was Kant tempted by this? The chapter diagnoses an equivocation on the term **universalizable**.

The contrast between Smith the auto mechanic and Isaac Newton clarifies the background. Smith works only with rules of thumb and treats each case as an isolated particular. Newton understands particulars by subsuming them under general principles. That capacity to see inner similarities between apparently different situations is a mark of rationality. Thought is rational to the extent that it is driven by knowledge of principles that hold generally and are not context-specific.

From this, Kant infers that an act is rational to the extent that it is driven by principles that can be universalized. Then he says the principle behind lying—“I can tell a lie and benefit from it”—cannot be universalized, and so is irrational.

But “universalizable” is being used in two different senses.

Suppose my decision to lie to Larry is, apart from ethics, the right move. I have weighed the pros and cons correctly, understood my own objectives honestly, and my reasoning is guided by a thorough grasp of general principles. In that respect I am a Newton, not a Smith.

Under those assumptions, the principle governing my action is:

- **non-universalizable** in the sense that it should not be universalized, morally speaking;
- but **universalizable** in the sense that it is guided by an understanding of principles that hold generally.

Kant slides from the second notion to the first. That is why his argument seems stronger than it is.

## The lasting insight: autonomy as the core

Yet the attempt is not a complete failure. The chapter insists that Kant’s deepest and most fruitful idea is not CI1 but the autonomy principle:

- **CI2\***: an act is good to the extent that it is autonomy-conducive and bad to the extent that it is heteronomy-conducive.

This is said to be, if not exactly true, a very good approximation to the truth. It explains why it is morally acceptable to undermine one person’s autonomy only to the extent necessary to prevent a greater violation of autonomy. We may attack or kill someone only insofar as doing so protects autonomy—our own or that of loved ones. We micromanage children’s lives because without such guidance they may fail to develop autonomy at all. We imprison criminals because, if we did not, they and others would produce greater violations of autonomy.

So morality is not captured by self-defeat under universalization. It is captured far more plausibly by autonomy and heteronomy.

## Rationality and autonomy

The final step is to explain why this autonomy-centered view is genuinely Kantian. Kant thinks what gives us value is our rationality. Rationality is what makes us better than animals. So the key question becomes: how are rationality and autonomy related?

The answer given is that **rationality is autonomy**.

- To be autonomous is to decide for oneself how to live.
- To be rational is to regulate one’s thought processes in accordance with logical norms.

So autonomy is deciding for oneself how to live; rationality is deciding for oneself how to think.

The obvious objection is that one might irrationally decide for oneself how to think. But the chapter responds by distinguishing **theoretical reason** from **practical reason**.

- **Theoretical reason** concerns drawing inferences.
- **Practical reason** concerns the relation between the inferences one draws and the intentions or decisions in which they eventuate.

Smith, who always infers the opposite of what the evidence supports, must first determine what the right inference is. In doing that, he is theoretically rational. His irrationality lies in what he does with the correct inference; that is practical irrationality. Brown, who decides simply to let beliefs arise spontaneously, has in effect decided not to decide for himself what to think. Once he lives that way, he is no longer rational, so he is not a genuine counterexample either.

The upshot is: deciding for oneself how to think always involves norm-governed regulation of thought. Rationality is therefore **intellectual autonomy**.

Practical autonomy works similarly. To be autonomous is to regulate one’s actions in accordance with norms one has adopted. The objection from Williams—who decides he will simply do whatever he wants—fails because once one abandons deliberation, one is not deciding anything. One is merely acting. Non-rational creatures do not choose; they react.

That is why the chapter distinguishes rational agents from dogs and infants. Dogs have intentions, but they do not deliberate. Their lives are programmed reactions to stimuli. Rational creatures need not consciously deliberate before every act, but their responses reflect prior choices structured by norms. The author’s example of the ice-cold beer makes this vivid: refraining from drinking it in the morning is not an instinctive reaction but the embodiment of prior deliberation about how to live.

Thus:

1. To be rational is to regulate thought by norms.
2. To be autonomous is to regulate action by norms.
3. The latter presupposes the former, since one must think well to know how to act in compliance with adopted norms.
4. Therefore autonomy is a special case of rationality, and rationality is autonomy.

## Agency, responsibility, and respect

This yields the chapter’s final and strongest Kantian claim. A being that does not make decisions is not an agent in the robust sense in which adult human beings are agents. Non-autonomous creatures have intentions, but those intentions are formed impersonal way, through structure, experience, and immediate context. Autonomous beings form their own intentions. They are therefore responsible for them. Agency in this robust sense is identical with rationality and with autonomy; and agency in this sense is identical with moral responsibility.

From this it follows that respect for a person’s autonomy is respect for his agency and thus for his existence insofar as he is, in the robust sense, a subject.

This does **not** establish that one’s own welfare necessarily consists in respecting other people’s autonomy. Kant’s argument to that conclusion fails. But it does establish something important:

- one’s welfare depends on, if it is not identical with, being moral to oneself;
- that is, on not encroaching on one’s own autonomy.

So Kant’s attempt to identify morality with self-interest is unsuccessful in its official argument, especially in the appeal to CI1. Yet it is powered by a cogent analysis of agency, rationality, and autonomy. That analysis survives the collapse of the universalization test, and it explains why the most defensible Kantian legacy lies in the claim that what is morally good is, in general, what is autonomy-conducive, and what is bad is what conduces to heteronomy.

title: Pleasure, Welfare, and Duty
blurb: Hedonism, egoism, utilitarianism, rule utilitarianism, and deontology assessed through value, rights, and autonomy.
body:
# Pleasure, Welfare, and Duty

## Hedonism: two doctrines under one name

The word **hedonism** is ambiguous. It names two distinct doctrines.

1. **Ethical hedonism**: one has an obligation to pursue one’s own pleasure, and no other obligations.
2. **Psychological hedonism**: human beings always seek pleasure; whenever a person acts, he acts in order to experience pleasure.

The distinction matters immediately. A person can coherently accept ethical hedonism without accepting psychological hedonism. Indeed, the text insists on something stronger: it would be incoherent to advocate ethical hedonism unless psychological hedonism were false. If psychological hedonism were true, then people would seek pleasure no matter what. In that case, there would be no point in telling people to pursue their own pleasure. A normative doctrine would become idle because the purportedly required behavior would already be guaranteed by a law of psychology.

Psychological hedonism does not deny that people sometimes deliberately forego immediate pleasures. Its claim is subtler. When people forego a pleasure, they do so only because they think the sacrifice necessary for greater pleasure later. So even apparent self-denial is explained as pleasure-seeking.

The central question is whether this explanatory doctrine is true.

## Intention, foreseen effect, and the physician case

The decisive distinction is between:

- doing something **with the intention** of bringing about X, and
- doing something **knowing** that X will result.

The example is precise. A physician must perform a lifesaving emergency procedure, but there is no anesthetic. He knows the patient will experience pain. Yet he does not perform the procedure **in order to inflict pain**. We know this because, if anesthetic were available, he would use it. This is the **doctrine of double effect**: the pain is foreseen, not intended.

This distinction is fatal to psychological hedonism if the latter treats every pleasant consequence as the intention of the act. Merely because an agent knows an act will produce pleasure, it does not follow that he acts in order to secure that pleasure.

The example of Smith, a latter day Mozart, makes the point. Suppose Smith knows that composing music brings him pleasure. It does not follow:

1. that he composes in order to bring himself pleasure, or
2. that his primary reason for composing is self-gratification.

Rather, he composes because he sees that composing has value. Because it has value, doing it brings him pleasure.

This order of explanation is crucial. Value comes first; pleasure follows. The pleasure is not what explains the valuing. The valuing explains the pleasure.

## Pleasure as a reflection of perceived value

The text’s claim is stronger than the mere denial of one reductive explanation. It offers a positive account of a large class of human action.

One derives pleasure from composing only if one sees value in it. If one thought composing a waste of time, one would not like it. The same applies to playing soccer, doing medical research, or writing treatises. People do not typically engage in such activities in order to bring themselves joy. They do them because they value them; and because they value them, the activities bring pleasure.

So the pleasure in such cases is best understood as a reflection of the agent’s belief that what he is doing has value.

This is why the psychological hedonist’s inversion is mistaken. The hedonist says: the value is a pretext, the pleasure the real aim. The text says: in central cases of meaningful action, the pleasure rides on the value, and cannot explain it.

## Mere pleasure and the base life

There are, of course, cases in which people act with the objective of experiencing pleasure. People drink alcohol and do drugs in order to feel pleasure. People take vacations and watch TV in order to experience pleasure. The author adds, of TV: “It doesn’t” have value, except insofar as having a good time qua having a good time has value. One does it because one likes to do it.

But these are precisely the acts we tend to regard as base. That evaluative fact is philosophically revealing.

Consider the contrast:

- Beethoven spends nearly every minute absorbed in composition.
- Party boy Jones spends his nights doing cocaine and his days sleeping off the effects.

Both enjoy themselves. Yet we admire Beethoven and revile Jones. Why? Because Beethoven composes in order to do something he values. It is not in order to make himself feel good that he composes; insofar as composing brings joy, that is because what he is doing has value. Jones, by contrast, does cocaine in order to have a good time. It is not to do something of value that he does it.

This contrast introduces a distinction between **joy** and **pleasure**. The words themselves encode moral judgment.

- **Joy** is what one feels when one feels good because what one is doing has value.
- **Pleasure** is what one feels when one feels good, but not because what one is doing has value.

Joy includes pleasure; they are not mutually exclusive. But there can be pleasure without joy—mere pleasure. And a life dedicated to mere pleasure is one that very few people, if any, regard as genuinely good. That is already a decisive reason to reject ethical hedonism.

## Why ethical hedonism is false

**Ethical hedonism** says that one’s moral obligation is to have a good time. But then consider Beethoven. Since it was not Beethoven’s intention in doing his important work to have a good time, ethical hedonism would require him to stop doing what he loved whenever doing so did not maximize his pleasure. Yet his life would obviously have been eviscerated had he been forced to give up composing. No viable ethical doctrine can require the Beethovens of the world to stop doing what they love in order to become munchkins like Jones.

The objection to ethical hedonism is not that pleasure lacks value. Pleasure has great value. The point is that it lacks an important kind of value. There are goods that are not exhausted by pleasure and in relation to which pleasure is secondary or derivative.

So ethical hedonism, superficially liberating, turns out on inspection to be dehumanizing and cruel.

## Mother Teresa, X, and Y

The same structure appears in the chapter’s variation on the argument.

Mother Teresa helped the poor because she saw value in it, not because she thought she would feel pleasure as a result. Because she saw value in feeding the poor, it gave her pleasure. But that was not why she did it.

Now compare X. X dislikes people, finds suffering mildly amusing, and is generally indifferent. After cranial surgery, however, he acquires a peculiar side effect: when he gives money to poor people, he experiences exquisite pleasure. The pleasure is not grounded in any belief that he is making the world better. Giving money to the poor causes pleasure in him the way shooting heroin causes pleasure in a user. The relation is strictly causal.

This case is philosophically useful because it isolates pleasure from value. X helps the poor only to the extent that doing so brings him pleasure. If hurting them produced comparable pleasure, he would not hesitate to hurt them. Mother Teresa, by contrast, would hesitate. Therefore:

1. Mother Teresa’s pleasure tracks her recognition of value.
2. X’s pleasure is merely causally attached to a behavior.
3. These are psychologically and morally different states.

The story of Y does the same work. Y thinks composing is a waste of time and does not even like music. Yet he has a knack for composition, and if he composes for a little while, he experiences a huge surge of pleasure. His relation to composing is like the heroin-user’s relation to heroin. The only difference is the mechanism: pen rather than syringe.

Beethoven’s joy in composing was not like Y’s. Beethoven valued composing, and that is why it made him feel good.

These cases are decisive against both psychological and ethical hedonism because they show that pleasure can either be:

- a reflection of value, or
- a merely causal reward detached from value.

The doctrines of hedonism erase that distinction, and with it the distinction between meaningful and base life.

## Egoism: psychological and ethical

The word **egoism** is ambiguous in exactly the same way.

1. **Ethical egoism**: one ought never act in a manner that is not self-interested.
2. **Psychological egoism**: one cannot act in a manner that is not self-interested; one’s sole intention in any act is to benefit from it.

The expected benefit may be simple pleasure or what the text calls an authentic enhancement of self. But the same criticism used against psychological hedonism applies here. It was in Beethoven’s self-interest to compose only because composing itself has value. If he did not recognize the value of composing, he would not see it as being in his interest.

The same goes for being on the Supreme Court. If one does not see value in being on it, it would mean nothing and would not appear to be in one’s interest. Thus what counts as one’s interest is parasitic on prior recognition of value. Psychological egoism gets the order backward.

The doctrine also faces counterexamples, foremost Mother Teresa. Advocates say she acted as she did because doing so made her feel good, and so she was really acting self-interestedly. But this repeats the same mistake. She would not have enjoyed those acts unless she saw them as valuable. She did them because she saw their value, and because they were valuable, doing them made her feel good. Again, that is very different from saying she did them in order to feel good.

Ethical egoism fails for parallel reasons. Mother Teresa helped people not because it was in her interest, but because she saw value in helping them. True, once she structured her life around that value, helping people came to be in her interest. Had she gone into investment-banking, becoming a good investment-banker would have become in her interest. But it was not **ab initio** in her interest to pursue either path. Interest follows commitment to value.

The chapter asks whether there are any cases where it is in one’s interest to do something that has no value beyond being in one’s interest. By definition, such acts would not involve recognizing value in anything beyond one’s self-interest. They would therefore resemble enjoyable but meaningless acts such as shooting heroin. It may indeed be in one’s interest to have a meaningless good time now and then. But a life consisting in nothing else would radically diminish oneself. Ethical egoism is therefore called incoherent.

## Utilitarianism and the problem of autonomy

**Utilitarianism** says that an act is good to the extent that it promotes human welfare and bad to the extent that it undermines it. It is an appealing doctrine. Helping people is good; hurting them is bad. But the chapter isolates serious problems.

The first two stories are canonical.

### Story 1: organ harvesting

You are a physician. To save five unhealthy people who need organ transplants, you must kill or vivisect four healthy people and transplant their organs into the five. Should you kill the four to save the five? Presumably not. Why not? Because it is a heinous violation of the autonomy of the four.

### Story 2: framing the innocent

A child has been murdered horribly. The real killer has fled to a country from which extradition would cause a devastating war. The public will riot unless someone is convicted. The police can frame an innocent person and thereby prevent disaster. Should they? Presumably not. Again, because it is wrong to violate the autonomy of the innocent person.

These cases suggest that there are acts that remain wrong no matter how much good comes of them. If so, this substantiates Kant’s position that goodness equals autonomy promotion and badness equals heteronomy promotion. **Heteronomy** here is the condition of being subject to another’s will rather than respected as a subject.

The chapter lists further problems with utilitarianism:

1. If everyone were always trying to maximize others’ welfare, everybody would be miserable, because no one would be doing what he wanted.
2. It cannot recognize the value of reading a book or listening to a good piano sonata except insofar as such acts help others.
3. It cannot accommodate the moral value of personal loyalties: saving a stranger rather than one’s devoted spouse of fifty years for an infinitesimal gain in aggregate welfare seems monstrous.
4. If everyone tried to improve the world with every single act by breaking rules whenever beneficial, institutions would collapse; judges who broke rules for justice would destroy the legal system.

## Rule utilitarianism and its attraction

**Rule utilitarianism** attempts to preserve the insight of utilitarianism while avoiding these objections. Its core idea is this: identify the set of rules that, if generally complied with, would lead to more happiness, and then comply with those rules.

So:

- physicians should not vivisect one person to save others, because general acceptance of such behavior would make life a horror;
- police should not frame innocent people, because routine framing would turn them into tormentors;
- people should not sacrifice all ambition or personal relationships, because general sacrifice of that kind would produce unfulfillment and destroy personal loyalties.

RU also illuminates talk of sovereignty and civil liberties. A nation’s “inviolable right to self-govern” can function as an abbreviation for a rule-utilitarian point: even when intervention would be justified in a particular case, a general permission to invade other nations would have terrible consequences. Likewise, the claim that people have “inviolable civil liberties” often means that practices acceptable on some occasion would be disastrous if normalized. Planting evidence against a serial killer may not in itself be a miscarriage of justice, but permitting such rule-bending would predictably lead to bona fide miscarriages and regressive social change.

So RU has real merit.

## Why rule utilitarianism is still false

Despite these merits, RU is said to be unsatisfactory. Its deepest flaw is that it makes rights and values contingent on ripple effects.

If RU were correct, a person’s right not to be vivisected would depend on the bad consequences of establishing a practice of vivisection. But surely vivisecting a person would be wrong even if it did not lead to more vivisection. Likewise:

- preventing Beethoven from composing would be wrong even without broader ripple effects;
- preventing people from favoring loved ones would be wrong even without social fallout.

These things have **intrinsic value**. Composing music is a good unto itself. Health, meaningful relationships, and life itself likewise have value not reducible to social consequences. RU can recognize only instrumental value. It is therefore systematically blind to what is actually valuable in Beethoven’s work, in health, and in intimate relations. For that reason, RU is false.

## Deontology, its strength, and its limit

**Consequentialism** is the doctrine that what makes an act good is that it has certain effects. Utilitarianism is one form of consequentialism: right action is action that maximizes welfare.

**Deontological** theories say instead that rightness consists in compliance with one’s duties and obligations to others. The example given is Kant’s claim:

- an act is wrong if it treats a person as an object, not a subject;
- an act is right if it treats a person as a subject, not an object.

So deontology ties rightness to respect, not merely to outcome.

The consequentialist says the ends justify the means. The deontologist rejects this. Children are ends unto themselves and are not to be used, even for the betterment of the human condition.

Yet deontology has limits. In low-stakes cases, it seems entirely plausible: you should keep a promised lunch date with an old friend even if breaking it would do slightly more good. A promise is a promise. But in high-stakes cases, consequentialism seems clearly correct: if you must break the lunch date to save a life, you should; if you must kill one person to save a million, you should.

This suggests that deontology, insofar as it sharply diverges from consequentialism, is incoherent. Letting a million perish to save one violates their rights. In that sense, utilitarianism can appear more deontological than deontology itself.

## Rule utilitarianism revisited and the unified view

At this point RU appears unstable. If, in hard cases, one must never break the rules, then RU is no longer utilitarian; it says rules are to be obeyed for their own sake, which is deontology. If one may break the rules when doing so prevents enough badness, then RU collapses into act-utilitarianism.

The concluding position is therefore a **unified approach**. The deontologist and consequentialist do not fundamentally disagree about what a moral world is. Both want a world in which rights are respected. A maximally good outcome is one in which rights are not violated. Their disagreement concerns how such a world is to be produced.

- The consequentialist says: do not follow rules blindly; do the right thing; do not hide behind protocol; be a hero, not a zero.
- The deontologist says: other things being equal, you will do more good by respecting rights and obligations than by violating them; good intentions that disregard limits pave the road to hell; do your duty; do not play God.

These are rival strategic attitudes toward the creation of a moral world, not wholly divergent conceptions of morality itself. The deontologist, so represented, resembles the rule-utilitarian; the consequentialist resembles the act-utilitarian. The final suggestion is that the disagreement between deontology and consequentialism is less profound than it is often taken to be.

title: Religion, Logic, and Euthyphro
blurb: Why philosophy says almost nothing about religion, except one decisive thing about morality and God.
body:
# Religion, Logic, and Euthyphro

## Philosophy and religion: almost no contact

The chapter’s governing claim is stark: philosophy has nothing to teach us about religion, except in one very specific respect. What passes as the **philosophy of religion** typically concerns not religion, but logical puzzles that happen to be illustrated by religious vocabulary.

Consider the familiar paradox about divine power:

1. Many hold that God is omnipotent, meaning that She can do anything.
2. If so, God can create some task that She cannot perform.
3. But if She can create such a task, then there is something She cannot do.
4. Therefore, She is not omnipotent.

This is labeled **OG**. But the point is that OG is no more about God than the following is about barbers:

1. Smith shaves all and only those who don’t shave themselves.
2. Does Smith shave himself?
   - If he does, then he doesn’t.
   - If he doesn’t, then he does.

This is **SG**. Both paradoxes arise from logical structure, specifically from difficulties involving **quantifiers**. A quantifier is an expression like “all,” “only,” “some,” or “there is.” The puzzle is not theological. It is logical.

The same diagnosis applies to classical arguments for God’s existence. They purport to prove something religious, but in fact they mostly reveal confusions about language, syntax, and inference.

## Aquinas’s first argument and quantifier ambiguity

Take Aquinas’s first argument:

1. Every event has a predecessor.
2. Therefore, there is some event that is the predecessor of every event.
3. That event is the first event.
4. Causes precede their effects.
5. So that first event, not being preceded by anything, was uncaused.
6. Since all events must be caused, that first event was a miracle and therefore the act of a deity.
7. Therefore, there is a God.

The key problem lies in the first sentence, “Every event has a predecessor.” It is **ambiguous**. More precisely, it is **syntactically ambiguous**: it can be parsed in more than one way. A sentence is syntactically ambiguous iff it can be grouped into phrases in more than one way.

The sentence can mean either:

- **(a1)** Given any event x, there is some event y such that y precedes x.
- **(a2)** There is some event x such that, for any event y, x precedes y.

These are radically different.

- (a1) says: each event has some predecessor.
- (a2) says: there is one event that precedes all events.

But Aquinas needs (a2) to reach the conclusion that there is a first event. And (a1) does not entail that conclusion.

The chapter’s example is the integers:

- Any given integer has a predecessor.
- But it does not follow that there is some one integer that precedes every other integer.

Likewise:

- Any given event may have a predecessor.
- But it does not follow that there is one event that precedes every other.

So if Aquinas means (a1), the argument fails. If he means (a2), then he has simply assumed the very point he is supposed to prove, since (a2) is just the claim that there is a first event.

Even granting, for argument’s sake, that there was a first event, it still does not follow—at least not for any obvious reason—that this event was the act of God. Perhaps belief in a first event is inconsistent with atheism; perhaps not. The point is that this would have to be demonstrated. Aquinas has not demonstrated it.

So the lesson is logical, not religious: we learn about ambiguity and invalid inference, not about God.

## Aquinas’s second argument and comparatives without absolutes

Aquinas’s second argument says, in effect:

1. There can’t be **comparatives** unless there are **absolutes**.
2. If I am wealthier than you, I am more like some absolutely wealthy entity than you are.
3. If I am better than you, I am more like some absolutely good entity than you are.
4. Some things are better than others.
5. Therefore, some things are more like some absolutely good thing than others.
6. Therefore, there is some absolutely good thing.
7. Therefore, there is a God.

Again the argument fails. The crucial mistake is to infer existence from comparative resemblance.

The chapter’s worked example is complexion. If Smith’s complexion is better than Brown’s, then one may say:

- **(i)** Smith’s complexion is more like that of a person with a perfect complexion than Brown’s.

But what follows is not:

- **(ii)** Somebody has a perfect complexion, and Smith’s complexion is more like that person’s than Brown’s is.

What follows is rather:

- **(iii)** Were there to be a person with a perfect complexion, then, other things being equal, Smith’s complexion would be more like that person’s complexion than Brown’s.

So a comparative need not commit us to an actual absolute. Likewise:

- From “Smith’s condition is more like that of some perfect entity’s than Brown’s” we are not entitled to infer that there exists some maximally good entity.
- What we get is only the conditional claim: were there to be such an entity, Smith’s condition would more closely resemble it.

Thus, contrary to Aquinas, there do not have to be absolutes for there to be comparatives.

This brings out another distinction. The ambiguity here is not **lexical ambiguity**, as in “Jerry is at the bank,” where “bank” has two meanings. Rather, it is again syntactic ambiguity: the sentence contains one vocabulary but admits multiple parsings.

So once more, the philosophical gain is logical and linguistic. We learn about sentence structure, not religion.

## Rational argument and the religious attitude

The chapter’s next central claim is that rational argument for or against religious belief is futile. Why? Because **religion is not science or logic**.

The contrast is drawn through Smith. Smith is not religious but is open-minded. He evaluates alleged evidence for God, discards bogus evidence, proportionates his confidence to what the evidence warrants, and remains prepared to revise his view if future evidence requires it.

That is the hallmark of a scientific attitude:

- belief constrained by current evidence,
- tentative in light of future findings,
- always revisable.

Even if Smith comes to believe that God exists, he is not thereby religious. As long as his belief is contingent on consistency with future data, it is a scientific, not a religious, stance.

A person may of course be both religious and scientific. Newton was. But to the extent that one’s attitude toward a proposition is deferential to future evidence, one is not, in that respect, religious.

This explains why attacks on religion that invoke facts and logic miss their target. They assume that religious belief is answerable to the same yardsticks as science. But a **religious attitude** is precisely one not marked by subservience to data and logic in that way. Hence anti-religious arguments often **beg the question**: they assume the standards whose authority religious mentality, insofar as it is religious, does not accept.

The chapter therefore says that attempts to understand religion in epistemological terms are misguided. Religious sentiment is better approached in **psychoanalytic** terms. Doctrines are often merely **foils**, stand-ins for attitudes or convictions not appearing *in propria persona*.

## Liberalized religion and dishonesty

The same line explains the rejection of attempts to liberalize religion by redefining God as love, truth, logic, or reason.

If someone says “God is love” and means only that there is love in the world, that is not belief in God. Freud, an atheist, believed people sometimes love other people. He even took libido to be a basic force of human psychology.

Similarly, one may say “God is logic” or “God is truth,” but many dedicated atheists believe in logic and truth. So these identifications evacuate the religious content.

The chapter’s blunt conclusion is:

- God does not mean that some inferences go through.
- God does not mean that some people love some people.
- Therefore God is not logic, truth, or love.

If your belief extends no further than belief in logic or libido, then you do not believe in God.

## “Never explain, never complain”
